regular.q: Priya is configuring a split-tunnel VPN for remote staff. What fundamentally distinguishes a split-tunnel VPN from a full-tunnel VPN?
choices: How much bandwidth the client's ISP provides
A split-tunnel VPN sends only traffic destined for the client's local device through the tunnel.
A split-tunnel VPN sends only traffic destined for the corporate network through the tunnel, while other traffic goes directly to the internet.
A full-tunnel VPN makes the client appear to be on the internet rather than the local network.
regular.exp: In a split-tunnel VPN, only traffic bound for the corporate/remote network is routed through the encrypted tunnel; everything else reaches the internet directly. A full-tunnel VPN instead routes all client traffic through the tunnel.

regular.q: Omar is choosing between a full-tunnel and split-tunnel VPN for a remote sales team. Which statement correctly describes the difference?
choices: Full-tunnel VPNs encrypt only traffic bound for internal servers.
Split-tunnel VPNs route every packet, including general web browsing, through the corporate network.
Split-tunnel VPNs send only corporate-bound traffic through the encrypted tunnel, while everything else reaches the internet directly.
Split-tunnel VPNs are inherently more secure than full-tunnel VPNs in every case.
regular.exp: A split-tunnel VPN routes only corporate-destined traffic through the tunnel; a full-tunnel VPN routes all traffic through it, which is more secure but consumes more bandwidth.

regular.q: Renata receives a laptop that a store manager picked up from a terminated employee's desk and kept in a locked cabinet for ten days before handing it over. What issue should Renata flag if this device may be used in litigation?
choices: The laptop cannot be imaged after being powered off for that long.
The laptop may no longer be subject to the organization's legal hold policy.
The laptop's storage may have degraded from being unpowered.
There is an undocumented gap in the chain of custody.
regular.exp: Because the laptop wasn't logged, secured, and transferred with documentation the moment it was recovered, there's an unaccounted-for period that breaks the chain of custody and undermines the evidence's integrity.

regular.q: A paralegal discovers that a seized external drive sat in an unlocked mailroom bin for two days before reaching the forensics team, with no record of who handled it. What evidentiary problem does this create?
choices: An undocumented gap in the chain of custody
Failure to place a legal hold
regular.exp: Any span of time where evidence handling isn't logged and controlled breaks the chain of custody, potentially making the evidence inadmissible or its integrity questionable.

regular.q: Wendell needs a network tap that keeps traffic passing through even during a prolonged power outage, with no electricity required. What should he deploy?
regular.exp: A passive fail-open tap needs no power at all to keep passing traffic through. Active taps rely on power (or battery backup) to remain open.

regular.q: A network technician needs a tap that has no electronic components and continues passing traffic even with zero power available. Which should be selected?
regular.exp: Passive taps are purely physical/electrical pass-throughs; 'fail-open' means the tap defaults to letting traffic flow when it loses power.

regular.q: Deshawn wants a single appliance that combines firewall filtering, antivirus/antimalware scanning, VPN termination, and intrusion prevention. What should he choose?
regular.exp: A Unified Threat Management (UTM) appliance bundles multiple security functions — firewall, AV, VPN, IPS — into a single device.

regular.q: Which device type packages firewalling, antimalware scanning, VPN concentration, and intrusion prevention together in one appliance?
choices: A next-gen firewall running a single module
regular.exp: UTM stands for Unified Threat Management: one appliance delivering several integrated security services at once.

regular.q: Yusuf needs to duplicate all traffic crossing a link without adding any CPU load to the switch it runs through. What's his best option?
choices: Install a tap and also enable port spanning.
regular.exp: A physical tap copies the signal independently of the switch's processor, adding no load. Port mirroring/SPAN, by contrast, consumes switch resources.

regular.q: Which method of duplicating traffic for monitoring has the smallest performance impact on the switch itself?
regular.exp: Taps are inline hardware that copy the signal without involving the switch's processing pipeline, unlike SPAN/port mirroring.

regular.q: Marguerite maintains a remote facility stocked with all the hardware needed to run IT operations, but current data copies must still be transported there during an actual outage. What kind of site is this?
regular.exp: A warm site has equipment staged and ready but still needs data restored or delivered; a hot site already has live, replicated data and is ready to take over instantly.

regular.q: A recovery facility already has servers, switches, and workstations installed, but staff must still load the latest backups onto it before it can take over operations. What type of DR site is this?
regular.exp: Warm sites fall between cold sites (nothing pre-staged) and hot sites (fully live and replicated) in both readiness and cost.

regular.topic: HSM vs TPM vs Secure Enclave
regular.q: Tobias needs to centrally generate, store, and manage cryptographic keys and certificates for every server in his organization. What appliance should he deploy?
regular.exp: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is a dedicated network appliance built for centralized, organization-wide key and certificate management. A TPM protects a single device, and Secure Enclave is Apple's device-level isolated environment.

regular.topic: HSM vs TPM vs Secure Enclave
regular.q: Which solution offers a network-attached appliance for generating and managing encryption keys and certificates across an entire fleet of systems?
regular.exp: HSMs are purpose-built for centralized, organization-scale cryptographic key management, unlike a TPM, which is bound to a single device.

regular.q: Kaori configured her routers and switches to be reachable only through a dedicated management VLAN tied to separate management interfaces. What approach is she using?
regular.exp: Placing management traffic on its own VLAN/interface, apart from production traffic, is out-of-band management achieved through network segmentation.

regular.q: An engineer wires a physically separate VLAN and interface used exclusively for administering network gear, kept apart from user traffic entirely. What best describes this design?
regular.exp: Segmenting management traffic onto its own dedicated VLAN/interface is a textbook out-of-band management design.

regular.q: Farah is told that one of the organization's core routers has reached end of life. What should she do?
choices: Wait to plan a replacement until a new model is announced.
Budget and plan for replacement well before end of support arrives.
Plan the replacement only after end of support has already passed.
regular.exp: Sound lifecycle planning means budgeting and scheduling replacement proactively, ahead of the end-of-support date, rather than reacting after support has already lapsed.

regular.q: A vendor announces that a firewall model will reach end-of-life in twelve months. What should the security team do now?
choices: Wait until support actually ends before starting the replacement process.
Start budgeting and planning for a replacement well before support ends.
Take no action since the device still functions.
regular.exp: Lifecycle management calls for planning and budgeting replacements ahead of the end-of-support deadline instead of reacting once it has already passed.

regular.q: Which of the following exercise types most closely resembles an actual disaster event?
regular.exp: A real failover actually shifts operations onto a backup system, making it the closest thing to a genuine event; tabletop exercises and simulations remain discussion- or scenario-based only.

regular.q: Which of these disaster recovery exercise types most closely mirrors a genuine live outage?
regular.exp: Only a real failover test actually shifts live operations onto backup infrastructure, unlike tabletop, walkthrough, or simulation exercises, which stay theoretical.

regular.q: Nadia is investigating an incident where a user submitted an internal-only URL into a web form, causing the server itself to fetch that URL and return sensitive internal data as output. What attack does this describe?
regular.exp: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) tricks the server into issuing unauthorized requests to internal or restricted resources on the attacker's behalf.

regular.q: An attacker feeds a crafted internal-network address into a web application's input field, causing the server to retrieve and display data from an internal-only endpoint. This describes:
regular.exp: The defining trait of SSRF is the server itself making an unintended request to an internal resource at the attacker's direction.

regular.q: Which of the following is LEAST likely to be a direct consequence of running an unsecured wireless network?
choices: SSID spoofing to conduct an on-path attack
regular.exp: A DDoS attack isn't a typical direct outcome of weak Wi-Fi security the way eavesdropping, SSID spoofing, and unauthorized access are.

regular.q: An open, unencrypted wireless network is LEAST likely to directly expose an organization to which of these?
regular.exp: A DDoS attack generally isn't a direct consequence of weak wireless security, unlike eavesdropping, spoofing, and unauthorized access.

regular.q: Hector wants to know whether he's allowed to destroy a stash of old customer records he found in storage. Which policy would answer his question most directly?
regular.exp: A data retention policy specifies how long records must be kept and when they may legally be destroyed.

regular.q: Which policy tells an employee exactly how long tax records must be preserved before they can legally be destroyed?
regular.exp: Retention schedules, part of the data retention policy, define the minimum and maximum periods records must be kept.

regular.q: Simone is designing a program to watch for common categories of anomalous user behavior. Which of the following is NOT one of the standard categories used in this kind of monitoring?
regular.exp: Anomalous-behavior monitoring efforts typically focus on risky, unexpected, and unintentional behavior; 'repeated' on its own isn't one of the standard categories.

regular.q: When classifying behavior for an insider-threat program, which of these is typically NOT one of the standard categories examined?
regular.exp: The standard categories are risky, unexpected, and unintentional behavior — not simply how often an action repeats.

regular.q: Anaya's team is running workloads in a platform-as-a-service (PaaS) environment. Per the shared responsibility model, which of the following is typically a shared responsibility in PaaS?
regular.exp: Under PaaS, identity infrastructure is commonly shared between provider and customer, while data and account ownership stay with the customer and the physical hosts remain the provider's responsibility.

regular.q: In a PaaS shared responsibility model, which area is usually split between the cloud provider and the customer, rather than belonging entirely to one side?
regular.exp: Identity infrastructure in PaaS is frequently a shared function — the provider supplies platform-level identity services, and the customer configures and uses them.

regular.q: Griffin wants to check systems in his data center for unpatched, insecure services but lacks administrative credentials on most of them. What kind of tool should he use?
regular.exp: A network vulnerability scanner can probe hosts remotely to identify unpatched or insecure services without needing local admin credentials on each one.

regular.q: An analyst must find outdated, vulnerable services across the network but has no login access to most hosts. What's the best tool for the job?
regular.exp: Network vulnerability scanners probe hosts over the network rather than locally, so they can detect many issues without host-level credentials.

regular.q: Devon ran a port scan against the company's public-facing web server and found ports 22, 80, and 443 exposed. Which of these poses the greatest security risk?
choices: None of these ports pose a significant risk.
regular.exp: Port 22 (SSH) exposed to the internet is the riskiest, since a successful compromise or brute force grants direct administrative shell access.

regular.q: A scan of an internet-facing host shows ports 22, 80, and 443 open. Which open port is the greatest security concern?
regular.exp: SSH grants remote administrative access, so leaving it exposed to the internet is far riskier than the standard web ports.

regular.q: Corinne administers her company's IPS. A threat intel feed just described a new attack targeting the web servers, which must stay online. What action lets her IPS help the most?
choices: Manually write a custom signature from the threat details to block the attack.
Generate trend reports based on the threat feed.
Use behavioral heuristics to stop all traffic to the web servers.
Send alerts whenever traffic matching the new exploit is seen.
regular.exp: Writing and deploying a custom signature lets the IPS actively block the known attack pattern while the servers remain online — active prevention rather than passive alerting.

regular.q: A threat feed publishes indicators for a new exploit targeting production web servers that can't be taken offline. What IPS action gives the strongest active protection?
choices: Build and deploy a custom blocking signature based on the indicators
Log the matching traffic for later review
regular.exp: A deployed blocking signature actively stops the attack, whereas alerting or logging alone only records that it happened.

regular.q: The VP of Marketing directs IT to begin taking daily backups of the campaign analytics data. The VP is functioning as an example of a:
regular.exp: A data owner holds ultimate accountability for a dataset and decides requirements like backup schedules, retention, and classification.

regular.q: A department head sets the rules for how sensitive customer records should be classified and protected. This person is acting as the:
regular.exp: Setting classification and protection requirements for a dataset is the role of the data owner, who bears accountability for it.

regular.q: A company wants to automatically orchestrate its response whenever malware is detected on a company device. What's the BEST way to implement this?
regular.exp: Escalation scripting/automation, in the style of SOAR playbooks, can automatically orchestrate response actions the moment malware is detected.

regular.q: A SOC wants a malware detection to automatically trigger endpoint isolation and open a ticket without a human intervening. What capability makes this possible?
regular.exp: SOAR-style escalation scripting automates the response workflow the instant a detection fires.

regular.q: A company is warned of a hypervisor flaw that would let a process on one virtual machine reach resources belonging to another VM on the same host. What best describes this vulnerability?
regular.exp: A VM escape lets code running in a guest VM interact with the hypervisor or with other VMs, breaking the isolation boundary between them.

regular.q: Which term describes a vulnerability that lets malicious code inside a VM break out and interact with the underlying host or sibling VMs?
regular.exp: VM escape is the specific term for breaking out of a virtual machine's isolation boundary.

regular.q: An aerospace parts manufacturer builds components used by both commercial and military customers. A proposed policy would allow employees to carry personal mobile devices onto the production floor. What is the MOST significant threat vector this change introduces?
choices: Unauthorized software running on rooted devices
Remote access clients installed on the mobile devices
Mobile operating systems that are out of date
regular.exp: In a sensitive manufacturing/defense environment, the dominant concern is data or IP exfiltration through device cameras, storage, or connectivity, not the other listed issues.

regular.q: A defense contractor is weighing whether to allow personal smartphones on a factory floor where proprietary schematics are on display. What is the primary security concern?
choices: Loss of intellectual property via device cameras or storage
regular.exp: The dominant risk in a sensitive manufacturing environment is IP leakage or exfiltration through cameras and storage on personal devices.

regular.q: What is the BEST way for an organization to verify the digital signature attached by an external mail server to an inbound message?
choices: Inspect the mail server's device certificate
regular.exp: DKIM publishes a public key in DNS that recipients use to verify the digital signature attached to outbound email.

regular.q: To confirm that a message claiming to come from a partner domain was actually signed and left unaltered by that domain's mail server, what should be checked?
regular.exp: DKIM's DNS-published public key lets a recipient verify both the message signature and its integrity.

regular.q: A security audit found usernames and passwords sitting in plain view within a packet capture. What did the audit uncover?
regular.exp: Plaintext credentials visible in a capture indicate an insecure, unencrypted protocol — such as Telnet, FTP, or HTTP — was in use.

regular.q: While reviewing a packet capture, an analyst finds login credentials sent in cleartext. This points to:
regular.exp: Cleartext credentials in transit are a direct sign that an unencrypted, insecure protocol was used.

regular.q: A logistics company built an in-house mobile app for shipment tracking. Developers want the app to detect revoked server certificates without generating any traffic to the CA over the corporate internet connection. What must be configured to enable this?
regular.exp: OCSP stapling has the server attach a timestamped, signed OCSP response directly to the TLS handshake, so the client never has to contact the CA itself.

regular.q: An administrator wants to cut down on how often clients query the CA directly for certificate revocation status, while still validating certificates in real time. What should be configured?
regular.exp: OCSP stapling shifts the revocation-check burden onto the server, cutting down on direct client-to-CA queries.

regular.q: A municipal agency is evaluating bids for a new contract, and one of the bidders turns out to be a firm owned by the agency director's brother. Which of the following describes this situation?
regular.exp: A close relative's ownership stake in a bidding company creates a conflict of interest in the procurement decision.

regular.q: During vendor selection, it comes to light that one of the bidding firms is partly owned by the procurement manager's spouse. This situation represents a:
regular.exp: A personal or financial relationship that could bias a business decision is a conflict of interest.

regular.q: A company is legally required to keep customer records stored within the same country as each customer's billing address. What term describes this requirement?
regular.exp: Data sovereignty refers to data being subject to, and often required to physically remain within, the laws of the country where it was collected.

regular.q: A regulation mandates that Canadian residents' personal data be stored only on servers physically located within Canada. This requirement is best described as:
regular.exp: A legal requirement tying data storage location to national or regional law is the definition of data sovereignty.

regular.q: An employee in the finance department can't connect to the wireless network. After entering a valid username and password, they get an error saying the credentials from the RADIUS server couldn't be validated against the root CA. The AP is set up with WPA3 encryption and 802.1X authentication. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: The laptop is assigned to the wrong VLAN
The laptop's wireless adapter doesn't support WPA3
The employee is out of wireless signal range
The client device is missing the proper certificate
regular.exp: An error about the CA/root certificate failing validation points to a missing or untrusted certificate on the client device, not signal strength, VLAN assignment, or a down RADIUS server.

regular.q: A contractor gets a certificate-trust error while joining a WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X) network, even though their username and password are accepted. What's the most likely cause?
choices: The client device is missing or doesn't trust the RADIUS server's CA certificate
The access point doesn't support WPA3
regular.exp: A trust error occurring after credentials are already accepted almost always points to a client-side certificate problem, not signal strength, VLAN, or AP capability.

regular.q: An administrator is upgrading the network to support 802.1X authentication. Which backend service would be the BEST choice to pair with it?
regular.exp: 802.1X typically relies on a RADIUS server that queries a directory service like LDAP to authenticate users and devices.

regular.q: To support centralized 802.1X authentication across both wired and wireless clients, which directory protocol is most commonly paired with the RADIUS server?
regular.exp: LDAP directories store the accounts that RADIUS checks against during 802.1X authentication.

regular.q: Which of the following are the main reasons an administrator would rely on a TPM when setting up full disk encryption? (Select TWO)
choices: It allows several volumes to be encrypted at once
It uses cryptographic keys burned into the hardware
It stores certificates in a network-attached hardware security module
It maintains a local copy of the certificate revocation list
It provides built-in protection against brute-force key-guessing attempts
regular.exp: TPMs contain unique, hardware-burned cryptographic keys and include anti-hammering/brute-force protections for the secrets they store.

regular.q: Which of these are defining characteristics of a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) used for full-disk encryption? (Select TWO)
choices: Hardware-bound cryptographic keys unique to that device
Built-in protection against brute-force attacks on stored keys
Support for encrypting an unlimited number of volumes
regular.exp: A TPM's defining features are device-bound, hardware-burned keys and hardware-level protection against brute-force key-guessing attempts.

regular.q: Fatima wants outbound mail from her domain to be verifiable as authentic and untampered, and she wants receiving mail servers to know exactly how to handle messages that fail those checks. Which protocol(s) should she deploy?
regular.exp: SPF validates which servers may send on the domain's behalf, DKIM signs messages for integrity, and DMARC tells receivers what policy to apply — together they provide complete email authentication.

regular.q: An organization wants to (1) confirm a message came from an authorized sending server, (2) verify it wasn't altered in transit, and (3) tell receiving domains what to do with mail that fails those checks. Which combination accomplishes all three?
regular.exp: Each protocol covers a different piece: SPF handles sender authorization, DKIM handles integrity, and DMARC handles policy and reporting.

regular.q: Malik needs to sanitize an SSD that has used full-disk encryption for its entire service life. What is the most effective way to make its data permanently unrecoverable?
choices: Overwrite the entire drive with binary 0s.
Perform a full reformat of the drive.
Overwrite the entire drive with random patterns of 1s and 0s.
Destroy the drive's encryption key, then issue the SATA secure erase command.
regular.exp: Cryptographic erasure — destroying the key — instantly makes encrypted data unrecoverable; paired with a secure erase command, it's the most effective, SSD-appropriate approach.

regular.q: An organization is decommissioning a self-encrypting SSD. What is the fastest, most effective way to guarantee the data can never be recovered?
choices: Overwrite the entire drive with zeros three times
Destroy the encryption key and issue a secure erase command
Physically wipe it with a magnetic degausser
regular.exp: Crypto-erase paired with a secure erase command is fast and effective for SSDs; degaussing has no effect since SSDs aren't magnetic media.

regular.q: What purpose does a load balancer's virtual IP serve?
choices: It's the address the load balancer uses internally to reach the load-balanced systems.
It's the single, front-facing address clients connect to.
It's a nonroutable address that lets the load balancer masquerade as multiple systems.
It's the set of TCP ports used to identify systems behind the load balancer.
regular.exp: The virtual IP (VIP) is the single, front-facing address clients connect to; the load balancer then distributes requests to the backend real IPs.

regular.q: Clients all connect to one published address, which then spreads requests across a pool of backend application servers. What is this published address called?
regular.exp: The VIP is the externally visible address that abstracts away the pool of backend servers behind it.

regular.q: Farida wants to defend against DNS cache poisoning and knows that digitally signing DNS responses for protected zones would help. What should she configure?
regular.exp: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records so resolvers can validate authenticity and integrity, preventing poisoning and spoofing.

regular.q: Which technology adds cryptographic signatures to DNS responses so a resolver can confirm the data hasn't been forged or altered in transit?
regular.exp: DNSSEC specifically validates the authenticity of DNS data via signatures; DoH and DoT only encrypt the transport of the query.

regular.q: Which governance model uses a bottom-up approach, delegating authority to individual business units to achieve cybersecurity objectives on their own?
regular.exp: Decentralized governance pushes decision-making authority down to business units; centralized governance keeps it at the top.

regular.q: In which governance structure do individual departments set and enforce their own security policies to meet overall goals, rather than following directives handed down from the top?
regular.exp: Decentralized governance delegates authority to individual business units rather than a central body.

regular.q: The network Deven is joining requires every device to defend itself against threats both from outside its local security zone and from other systems sharing that same zone. What design concept mandates this?
regular.exp: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust anywhere, including within the same segment — every device must verify and protect itself regardless of network location.

regular.q: A security architecture requires continuous verification for every connection, even between two devices on the same internal VLAN, rather than assuming trust based on network location. This best describes:
regular.exp: Zero trust removes implicit trust based on network location, requiring verification everywhere.

regular.q: Bianca wants an informal way to document the relationship between her department and an internal IT service team supporting a different business unit within the same company. What agreement type fits best?
regular.exp: A Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) is an informal, non-binding document outlining mutual goals — well suited to intra-company arrangements.

regular.q: Two teams within the same company want to record expectations for a shared internal tool informally, without drafting a legally binding contract. Which agreement type fits best?
regular.exp: MOUs are informal and typically used between internal groups rather than external contractual parties.

regular.q: Nathaniel has enabled UEFI boot attestation on the servers he manages. What actually happens during boot attestation?
choices: Each boot component is checked against a list of signed, known-good software before it loads.
The system builds a chain of trust from component to component as it loads during boot.
The system reports the trustworthiness of the software it ran to a separate verification platform once boot completes.
regular.exp: Attestation specifically means reporting or proving boot integrity to a separate verifying platform after the boot process finishes — distinct from secure boot (checking signatures) or measured boot (building a chain of trust).

regular.q: Once a server finishes booting, it sends cryptographic measurements of its boot sequence to a remote verification service to prove nothing was tampered with. What is this process called?
regular.exp: Attestation is the act of reporting boot integrity measurements to an external verifier.

regular.q: Priyanka works the front desk at a hotel chain and regularly fields guest requests and complaints over phone and email. Which type of training would best prepare her to recognize social engineering and pretexting attempts?
regular.exp: Role-based training tailors content to the specific risks of a job function — customer-facing staff need pretexting and social engineering awareness specific to their role.

regular.q: An accounts-payable clerk receives training focused specifically on invoice fraud and business email compromise, tailored to risks unique to that job function. What type of training is this?
regular.exp: Training tailored to a specific job's risk exposure is role-based training.

regular.q: Marcus is reviewing a draft information security policy. Which of the following statements would fit better in a different, more granular document?
choices: All remote connections to payroll systems must use multifactor authentication.
The company designates the chief information security officer as the individual with primary responsibility for information security.
The chief information security officer is granted authority to issue specific requirements implementing this policy.
The company considers cybersecurity and compliance critical to the business.
regular.exp: Specific, technical requirements — like a mandate to use MFA — belong in a standard or procedure document, not the high-level policy itself.

regular.q: Which statement below is too specific and technical to belong in a high-level information security policy, and should instead live in a standard or procedure?
choices: The organization designates a CISO responsible for security.
All remote database connections must use TLS 1.2 or higher.
Cybersecurity is a critical business priority for the organization.
The CISO may issue supporting requirements under this policy.
regular.exp: Policies state intent and authority at a high level; specific technical mandates belong in standards or procedures beneath them.

regular.q: Wendy discovered that the organization is vulnerable to a downgrade attack. After discussing it with her director, they agree that accepting the risk is the appropriate response. What should Wendy do next?
regular.exp: When a risk is accepted, the decision and its rationale must be formally documented for accountability and future review.

regular.q: After a risk assessment, leadership decides that mitigating a low-impact finding costs more than it's worth and chooses to accept the risk instead. What must happen next?
choices: Formally document the risk acceptance decision.
Escalate to the board for remediation funding.
regular.exp: Accepted risks must still be documented for governance, audit trails, and future reassessment.

regular.q: Which of the following environments is LEAST susceptible to an injection attack?
regular.exp: LDAP, SQL, and XML all interpret structured command or query syntax and are common injection targets; a CASB is a security control, not a query-based data environment.

regular.q: SQL, LDAP, and XML are all common injection targets because they interpret structured input as commands. Which of the following is NOT typically vulnerable to this class of attack?
regular.exp: A CASB enforces cloud access policy; it isn't a query or command interpreter the way SQL, LDAP, and XML are.

regular.q: Bianca is concerned that a web application at her company allows unvalidated redirects. Which approach would best minimize the risk of this attack?
choices: Restricting redirects to her organization's own domain
regular.exp: Restricting or allow-listing redirect targets to trusted domains directly prevents open-redirect abuse.

regular.q: To stop attackers from abusing a trusted site's redirect parameter to send victims to a malicious external site, what mitigation is most effective?
choices: Restrict allowed redirect destinations to the organization's own domain(s)
regular.exp: Only allow-listing legitimate redirect destinations closes an open-redirect vulnerability.

regular.q: Which of the following situations would be described as Shadow IT?
choices: Using a product the vendor has discontinued
regular.exp: Shadow IT is technology or systems used without IT or security's approval or visibility — an unapproved repository fits that definition.

regular.q: A marketing team begins using a personal file-sharing account to swap creative assets because the approved system is 'too clunky,' without telling IT. This is an example of:
regular.exp: Unsanctioned tools adopted outside IT's knowledge or control are the definition of shadow IT.

regular.q: Which of the following tools is an exploitation framework commonly used by penetration testers?
regular.exp: Metasploit is a well-known exploitation framework used to develop and launch exploit code against target systems.

regular.q: A red team lead needs a tool built specifically to develop, weaponize, and launch exploit code against a catalog of known vulnerabilities during an engagement. Which tool fits this need?
regular.exp: Metasploit is purpose-built as an exploitation framework, unlike the packet analysis, port scanning, or wireless-cracking tools listed.

regular.q: Odalys manages her organization's cloud server instances, which currently aren't tagged with the identity of the person responsible for each one. What is the primary risk of leaving this unaddressed?
regular.exp: Without ownership tags, unused and forgotten VM instances accumulate uncontrolled — this is VM/resource sprawl, an asset management problem.

regular.q: A cloud account has hundreds of running instances with no owner tags or lifecycle tracking, many of which nobody remembers spinning up. This is best described as:
regular.exp: Uncontrolled accumulation of untracked VM or cloud resources is VM sprawl.

regular.q: Rosalind is the CEO of a mid-sized logistics company and wants assurance about the effectiveness of internal controls while keeping costs down. Which type of audit should she consider?
regular.exp: An internal audit uses in-house staff, making it lower cost than external or third-party audits while still providing management assurance.

regular.q: A controller wants recurring assurance that financial controls are working properly, without paying for outside auditors every quarter. What audit type best fits this need?
regular.exp: Internal audits are conducted by an organization's own employees, avoiding the expense of external auditors.

regular.q: Naomi uses a cloud service that runs her code only in response to discrete triggering events and bills her based on the actual compute consumed during each execution. What term describes this service?
regular.exp: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) — such as AWS Lambda — runs code per event and bills per execution; it's a more specific subset of PaaS.

regular.q: A developer writes small snippets of code that only run in response to specific triggers, such as a file upload, with billing based purely on execution time and resources used. This model is called:
regular.exp: Event-driven, per-execution billing is the defining trait of FaaS.

regular.q: When feasible, which of the following approaches is the most effective way to defeat injection attacks?
regular.exp: Allow lists — permitting only known-good input patterns — are more effective than block lists, which can be bypassed by unanticipated malicious input.

regular.q: Which input validation strategy is generally considered strongest against injection attacks because it only permits explicitly approved input patterns?
regular.exp: Allowlisting is the strongest approach since it defines exactly what's permitted rather than trying to enumerate every possible bad pattern.

regular.q: Yolanda needs a digital certificate for a new web server going live this afternoon, and she has no existing relationship with any CA. What type of certificate can she obtain fastest?
regular.exp: Domain Validation (DV) certificates only require automated proof of domain ownership, making them the fastest to obtain.

regular.q: A startup needs HTTPS on a new website today and has no prior relationship with any certificate authority. Which certificate type is typically issued fastest, through automated validation?
regular.exp: DV certificates are issued almost instantly through automated domain-ownership checks, unlike OV or EV, which require manual vetting.

regular.q: A ransomware crew encrypts a hospital's billing systems and demands payment for the decryption key. Which threat actor category does this group most likely belong to?
regular.exp: Organized crime groups are financially motivated, running operations like ransomware, fraud, and theft. Hacktivists are driven by ideology, nation-states pursue espionage or strategic goals, and shadow IT isn't a threat actor at all.

regular.q: Investigators trace a wave of business email compromise scams back to a criminal syndicate that profits directly from each successful wire transfer fraud. What category of threat actor is this?
regular.exp: Financial motivation is the defining trait of organized crime threat actors.

regular.q: An administrator is configuring how technicians log into wireless access points and switches. Rather than use local accounts on each device, the admin wants every login request routed to a centralized database. What is the BEST way to implement this?
regular.exp: AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) frameworks like RADIUS or TACACS+ centralize authentication for network device logins.

regular.q: A company wants all switch and router administrator logins authenticated against a central server rather than local device accounts, with a log of who did what. What framework provides this?
regular.exp: AAA centralizes authentication, authorization, and accounting for network device access.

regular.q: A company owns a vending machine controller that offers no way to access its operating system and no method for updating its firmware. What best describes this device?
regular.exp: A purpose-built, closed device with no user-accessible OS or firmware update path is a classic embedded system.

regular.q: A parking garage's ticket dispenser has no accessible operating system, no way to patch firmware, and runs a single fixed function. What best classifies this device?
regular.exp: Closed, purpose-built, non-upgradable devices are classified as embedded systems.

regular.q: A vulnerability scan of the company's internet-facing servers flags several Sun Java Runtime Environment (JRE) vulnerabilities, but the server administrator confirms JRE was never installed on that host. What is the BEST way to handle this finding?
choices: Install the latest version of JRE on the server
Quarantine the server and scan it for malware
Harden the operating system of the web server
Document and dismiss the JRE finding as a false positive
regular.exp: Since JRE isn't actually installed, this is a false positive — the correct action is to document and dismiss it as such after verification.

regular.q: A vulnerability scanner flags a critical Apache Struts vulnerability on a server, but investigation confirms Struts was never installed on that host. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Document and dismiss it as a false positive
regular.exp: After confirming the software isn't present, the finding should be documented and dismissed as a false positive.

regular.q: Which of the following is the process of replacing sensitive data with a non-sensitive, functional placeholder?
regular.exp: Tokenization substitutes sensitive data with a non-sensitive token that maps back to the original only through a secure lookup vault.

regular.q: A payment gateway replaces credit card numbers with randomly generated reference values that have no mathematical relationship to the originals, but can be mapped back through a secure vault. This technique is:
regular.exp: Tokens are non-derivable substitutes that require a secure lookup table to reverse — that's tokenization, distinct from masking (partial obscuring) or hashing (one-way, irreversible).

regular.q: A courthouse wants visitors requesting access to a restricted records room to prove their identity using two distinct factors before entry is granted. Which of the following would actually satisfy that multi-factor requirement?
choices: A USB drive with full-disk encryption
A copy of the employee handbook
A smart card paired with a photo ID
regular.exp: A smart card (something you have) combined with a picture ID for visual identity verification supports multi-factor style authentication; the other options aren't authentication factors.

regular.q: A security auditor is reviewing a facility's entry procedures and needs to identify which control actually functions as multi-factor authentication rather than simple access control or paperwork. Which one qualifies?
choices: A smart card combined with photo ID verification
regular.exp: Only the smart card plus photo ID combination represents authentication factors; the others are access control or policy, not authentication.

regular.q: A company's network team is asked to build a site-to-site IPsec tunnel to a newly signed business partner. Which security risk is MOST important to consider first?
regular.exp: Connecting directly to a new external partner's network introduces third-party/supply chain risk — their security posture now affects yours.

regular.q: Before establishing a direct network connection, such as a site-to-site VPN, with a new vendor, what category of risk becomes most relevant to assess?
regular.exp: Direct connectivity to a third party's network is a classic supply chain risk scenario.

regular.q: A company's HR department keeps a roster of employees enrolled in the corporate retirement plan. An outside investment firm uses this roster to manage each employee's account. What role does this investment firm play?
regular.exp: A data processor handles data on behalf of, and per the instructions of, the data controller or owner — here, the outside firm processes employee data on the company's behalf.

regular.q: A payroll vendor receives employee salary data from a client business and processes it strictly according to that business's instructions to run payroll. The payroll vendor is acting as the:
regular.exp: Processing data on another organization's behalf and instruction is the definition of a data processor.

regular.q: A logistics firm runs a route-planning application and its database inside a virtualized cloud environment. What is the BEST way to back up these services?
regular.exp: Snapshots capture the full state of a virtualized instance at a point in time, making them the standard backup method in cloud and virtual environments.

regular.q: An engineer needs to capture the exact, complete state of a cloud-hosted database VM at a specific moment before applying a risky schema migration. What backup method should be used?
regular.exp: Snapshots are the go-to point-in-time backup method for VMs.

regular.q: A procurement officer is reviewing cloud vendor documentation and finds a chart mapping exactly which security duties the vendor performs versus which ones the customer must handle. What is this document called?
choices: A visual summary of cloud provider accountability
Identification of tasks at each step of a project plan
A list of cybersecurity requirements based on identified risks
regular.exp: A responsibility (or shared responsibility/RACI) matrix visually maps which party is accountable for which security functions, common in cloud provider relationships.

regular.q: A CISO negotiating a new SaaS contract wants a single document that visually spells out exactly which security tasks the vendor owns versus which ones her own team must handle. What should she request?
regular.exp: The responsibility matrix specifically maps out who owns which security function.

regular.q: An administrator is building out a company-wide authentication system. What is the best choice for validating every username and password against a single source?
regular.exp: LDAP directories are the standard centralized store for validating usernames and passwords across an authentication system.

regular.q: An organization wants a single centralized directory service that authentication systems can query to validate every employee's username and password. What should be used?
regular.exp: LDAP is the standard protocol and service for centralized, directory-based credential validation.

regular.q: A company has drawn up an itemized list of tasks a contracted vendor must complete. Once the work is finished, this document will be used to verify everything was done. What kind of agreement is this?
regular.exp: A Statement of Work (SOW) itemizes the deliverables and tasks a vendor must complete, and is used afterward to verify the work was done.

regular.q: A contract spells out the exact deliverables, milestones, and tasks a contractor must complete, and will later be used to verify the project was finished as agreed. This document is a:
regular.exp: An SOW defines the concrete scope of work to be validated against upon completion.

regular.q: A company is updating components within the control plane of its zero-trust implementation. Which of the following would be part of this update?
regular.exp: In zero-trust architecture, the policy engine (along with the policy administrator) sits in the control plane; the policy enforcement point sits in the data plane.

regular.q: In a zero-trust architecture, which component belongs to the control plane, responsible for evaluating access requests against policy rather than enforcing the decision itself?
regular.exp: The policy engine makes the access decision in the control plane; the enforcement point carries it out in the data plane.

regular.q: An administrator wants to monitor every outbound internet connection made by internal users for malicious software. Which of the following would provide this functionality?
regular.exp: A forward proxy sits between internal clients and the internet, allowing inspection and filtering of all outbound traffic.

regular.q: To inspect and filter every outbound web request leaving the corporate network before it reaches the internet, what should be deployed?
regular.exp: Forward proxies mediate outbound client-to-internet traffic; reverse proxies mediate inbound traffic to internal servers.

regular.q: An administrator configured MAC filtering on the corporate access point, but the access logs still show unauthorized users on the network. What should the administrator configure to prevent this going forward?
choices: Remove unauthorized MAC addresses from the filter
regular.exp: MAC addresses are trivially spoofed, so filtering alone is weak; enabling strong encryption and authentication (WPA3) actually secures access.

regular.q: A coworking space's wireless network relies only on MAC address filtering, yet unauthorized guests keep connecting because attackers are spoofing the allowed addresses. What should the network operator actually implement to fix this?
choices: Add more MAC addresses to the allow list
regular.exp: Since MAC filtering is trivially bypassed via spoofing, real encryption and authentication (WPA3) is the actual fix.

regular.q: A consortium of manufacturers uses blockchain technology to track raw materials as they move between companies. Where would a member of the consortium find these tracking details?
regular.exp: The distributed ledger is the shared, immutable record of blockchain transactions where all parties can view tracking history.

regular.q: A furniture manufacturer's blockchain-based tracking system lets every partner see a shared, tamper-evident history of each component transfer between factories. Where is that shared history actually stored?
regular.exp: The distributed ledger is the core blockchain data structure recording all transactions.

regular.q: A company runs two independent applications in its data center. The security team must guarantee that no communication whatsoever is possible between them. What's the BEST way to implement this requirement?
regular.exp: An air gap provides complete physical and network isolation, guaranteeing no communication path exists — stronger than logical separation via a firewall or VLAN.

regular.q: A requirement mandates that two systems have absolutely zero possibility of network communication between them, not merely filtered or restricted traffic. What architecture achieves this?
regular.exp: Only a true air gap, with no physical network connection, guarantees zero communication; VLANs and firewalls are logical controls that could theoretically be misconfigured.

regular.q: A hospital's lab results system must guarantee that no result is altered without detection as it moves between systems. Which principle of the CIA triad is being prioritized?
regular.exp: Integrity ensures data isn't modified or corrupted in an unauthorized way; hashing and checksums are common controls that support it.

regular.q: An online retailer adds redundant servers across multiple data centers so customers can always finish checkout, even during a regional outage. Which leg of the CIA triad does this primarily support?
regular.exp: Availability ensures systems and data remain accessible when needed; redundancy and failover are classic availability controls.

regular.q: A company wants to ensure that a manager who digitally signs a purchase approval cannot later deny having done so. Which security concept does this address?
regular.exp: Non-repudiation uses mechanisms like digital signatures to prevent someone from denying an action they took.

regular.q: Which control provides proof of a message's origin and integrity, preventing the sender from later claiming they never sent it?
regular.exp: Digital signatures cryptographically bind a sender's identity to a message, enabling non-repudiation.

regular.q: An employee enters a password and then must also tap a hardware security key to finish logging in. Which two authentication factor categories are being combined?
choices: Something you know and something you have
Something you are and somewhere you are
Something you do and something you have
Something you know and something you are
regular.exp: A password is something you know; a hardware security key is something you have. Combining distinct categories, not just methods, is what makes it true MFA.

regular.q: A banking app requires a fingerprint scan in addition to a PIN before approving a transfer. Which authentication factor does the fingerprint scan represent?
regular.exp: Biometrics like fingerprints represent the 'something you are' factor.

regular.q: A CISO compares the organization's current security posture against a target framework like NIST CSF to identify missing controls before drafting a remediation roadmap. What is this process called?
regular.exp: A gap analysis compares the current state to a desired state, often defined by a framework or standard, to identify what's missing.

regular.q: Before pursuing ISO 27001 certification, an organization documents which required controls it already has and which it's missing. What activity is this?
regular.exp: Identifying the difference between current controls and a target standard's requirements is a gap analysis.

regular.q: A data center wants to stop a vehicle from ramming through the front entrance while still letting pedestrians walk through freely. What should be installed?
regular.exp: Bollards are short, sturdy vertical posts designed to stop vehicle-borne attacks without impeding pedestrians.

regular.q: A secure facility needs to guarantee that only one authenticated person can pass through a door at a time, preventing tailgating. What should be installed?
regular.exp: An access control vestibule (mantrap) uses two interlocking doors so only one verified person passes through at a time, preventing tailgating.

regular.q: A threat intel team spins up a deliberately weak-looking database server, kept isolated from real production systems, solely to lure attackers in and study their tactics. What is this system called?
regular.exp: A honeypot is a decoy system designed to lure attackers away from real assets and reveal their tactics.

regular.q: To detect insider data theft, a company plants a fake file named 'Merger_Plans_Confidential.xlsx' on a file share and configures an alert if it's ever opened. What is this technique called?
regular.exp: A honeyfile is a decoy file planted to detect unauthorized access; opening it triggers an alert since no legitimate process should ever touch it.

regular.q: Before a firewall rule change goes live in production, it must be reviewed by a change advisory board, scheduled during an approved maintenance window, and paired with a documented backout plan. What process ensures this?
regular.exp: Change management governs how changes are proposed, approved, scheduled, and rolled back if needed, reducing the risk of unplanned outages.

regular.q: A patch deployment fails and causes an outage. Because a rollback procedure was documented and pre-approved, the team restores service within minutes. What part of change management made this possible?
regular.exp: A backout plan defines exactly how to reverse a change if it causes problems, and is a required part of formal change management.

regular.q: A government agency wants its analyst workstations to run only a pre-approved catalog of software, silently blocking everything else, including any tool not on that list. What approach accomplishes this?
regular.exp: An allow list permits only pre-approved software or traffic and blocks everything else by default, which is more restrictive and secure than a deny list.

regular.q: A campus IT department maintains a catalog of known-malicious programs that are specifically barred from running, while every other application remains permitted by default. What application control approach is this?
regular.exp: Deny listing blocks specifically known-bad items while allowing everything else by default — the opposite approach to allow listing.

regular.q: Before a certificate authority will issue a certificate for a new mail server, the administrator must generate a file containing the public key and identifying details to submit for signing. What is this file called?
regular.exp: A CSR contains the public key and organizational details, submitted to a CA to request a signed certificate.

regular.q: A company wants one certificate that secures shop.example.com, blog.example.com, and status.example.com without issuing a separate certificate for each. What type of certificate should they request?
regular.exp: A wildcard certificate (e.g., *.example.com) covers all first-level subdomains of a domain with a single certificate.

regular.q: Two branch offices need to exchange a large volume of data quickly, so they rely on a single shared secret key for both encrypting and decrypting it. What type of cryptography is this?
regular.exp: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encrypting and decrypting, and is much faster than asymmetric encryption — ideal for bulk data.

regular.q: An online store uses a public/private key pair so anyone can encrypt checkout data with the public key, but only the server holding the private key can decrypt it. What type of cryptography is this?
regular.exp: Asymmetric (public-key) encryption uses a mathematically linked key pair, commonly used for key exchange and digital signatures.

regular.q: A database stores passwords by running them through a one-way function that produces a fixed-length output which cannot practically be reversed. What is this technique called?
regular.exp: Hashing is a one-way transformation that produces a fixed-size digest; it cannot be decrypted back to the original input.

regular.q: To defend against precomputed rainbow table attacks on stored password hashes, a developer appends a unique random value to each password before hashing it. What is this called?
regular.exp: Salting adds a unique random value to each password before hashing, making precomputed rainbow tables ineffective.

regular.q: A company encrypts customer records sitting on its database server's disk, even though no application is currently reading or writing them. Which data state is being protected?
regular.exp: Data at rest refers to data stored on media, such as disks or backups, that is not actively moving or being processed.

regular.q: A checkout page uses TLS to protect a customer's payment details as they travel from the browser to the server. Which data state does TLS primarily protect?
regular.exp: Data in transit is data actively moving across a network; TLS encrypts it during that movement.

regular.q: A defense contractor labels a document 'Confidential' to signal it needs more protection than 'Public' data but less than 'Secret' data. What is this labeling process called?
regular.exp: Data classification assigns sensitivity labels, such as public, internal, confidential, or restricted, to guide how data must be handled and protected.

regular.q: Which data classification level would typically apply to a company's publicly posted press release?
regular.exp: Public classification applies to information intended for open, unrestricted distribution.

regular.q: A security camera that records footage for later investigation, but does nothing to stop an attacker while the incident is happening, is an example of which type of control?
regular.exp: Detective controls identify and record that an incident occurred; they don't prevent it from happening.

regular.q: A posted sign reading 'These premises are monitored by security cameras' is meant mainly to discourage someone from attempting a break-in in the first place. What type of control is this?
regular.exp: Deterrent controls discourage attackers from attempting an action in the first place, often through psychological effect.

regular.q: A router ACL that blocks inbound traffic to a specific port is an example of which control category?
regular.exp: Technical controls are implemented through technology or systems, such as firewalls, encryption, and access control lists.

regular.q: A written policy requiring annual risk assessments, approved and enforced by senior leadership, is an example of which control category?
regular.exp: Managerial controls are administrative in nature — policies, procedures, and governance decisions made by management.

regular.q: A file server uses a RAID configuration that stripes data across several disks with distributed parity, letting the array survive one disk failure. What RAID level is this?
regular.exp: RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity across at least three disks, tolerating a single disk failure without data loss.

regular.q: Which RAID level offers no redundancy at all, maximizing performance by striping data across disks with no parity or mirroring?
regular.exp: RAID 0 stripes data for performance but offers zero fault tolerance — losing any single disk loses all the data.

regular.q: A booking platform runs on two identical servers behind a load balancer, so if one fails, the other keeps serving customers without interruption. What concept does this illustrate?
regular.exp: High availability designs eliminate single points of failure so a system keeps operating despite a component failure.

regular.q: Which metric describes the percentage of time a system is expected to be operational, often expressed in 'nines' such as 99.99%?
regular.exp: Availability, usually expressed as a percentage of uptime, measures how consistently a system remains accessible.

regular.q: A backup job captures only the data changed since the previous backup every night, keeping nightly backups fast but stretching out restores since every increment must be applied in order. What backup type is this?
regular.exp: Incremental backups capture only data changed since the last backup of any type, requiring the full backup plus every incremental since to restore.

regular.q: A backup job captures everything changed since the last full backup, no matter how many days have passed, so a restore only needs the last full backup plus the most recent one of this type. What backup type is this?
regular.exp: Differential backups capture everything changed since the last full backup, growing larger each day but simplifying restores to just two backup sets.

regular.q: A colocation facility needs to keep servers running during a brief outage while its generator spins up. What device provides this short-term bridge power?
regular.exp: A UPS provides immediate, short-duration battery backup power, bridging the gap until a generator can take over for longer outages.

regular.q: A regional data center needs to stay operational through a multi-day utility outage caused by a hurricane. What is the primary long-term power solution it needs in place?
choices: An onsite generator with fuel supply
regular.exp: Generators provide sustained power through extended outages, while UPS units only cover the short gap until the generator starts.

regular.q: A well-resourced group with custom-built tools and the patience to stay undetected for months is attacking an energy-sector company. What attribute best distinguishes this actor from a typical opportunistic attacker?
choices: Purely ideological motivation with no capability
regular.exp: Nation-state and APT-level actors are typically characterized by high sophistication, significant funding, and persistence — distinct from unskilled or opportunistic attackers.

regular.q: An attacker with little technical skill downloads a pre-built exploit tool and fires it at random targets without understanding how it actually works. What term describes this type of actor?
regular.exp: An unskilled attacker, formerly called a 'script kiddie,' uses existing tools without deep technical understanding, unlike sophisticated nation-state or organized crime actors.

regular.q: An employee who was just denied a raise deliberately corrupts a shared database right before resigning. What motivation best describes this attack?
regular.exp: Acting out of personal grievance against the employer is classic revenge motivation, common in insider threat scenarios.

regular.q: A state-sponsored group quietly infiltrates a foreign ministry's network solely to collect classified diplomatic cables, without disrupting or damaging anything. What is the primary motivation?
regular.exp: Espionage involves covertly gathering sensitive or classified information, typically for strategic or intelligence advantage.

regular.q: An attacker sends a text message impersonating a package delivery service, asking the recipient to click a link and pay a small redelivery fee. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: Smishing is phishing conducted via SMS/text message. Vishing uses voice calls, and generic phishing usually refers to email.

regular.q: An attacker phones an employee, posing as the help desk, and convinces them to read their password aloud over the call. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: Vishing, or voice phishing, is social engineering carried out over a phone call.

regular.q: An attacker spoofs a company's controller's email account and sends accounts payable an urgent instruction to wire funds to a new vendor account. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: BEC involves impersonating or compromising a trusted executive's email to trick employees into fraudulent financial transfers.

regular.q: Which social engineering attack specifically targets accounting or HR staff using a spoofed or compromised executive email account to authorize fraudulent wire transfers?
regular.exp: BEC is specifically defined by impersonating a trusted internal figure via email to trigger financial fraud.

regular.q: An attacker compromises a specialty trade-association website that employees of a target company routinely visit, planting malware that infects visitors' machines. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: A watering hole attack compromises a website the target audience is known to visit, rather than attacking them directly.

regular.q: Which attack strategy relies on infecting a trusted third-party site that a specific group of targets is likely to visit, rather than sending anything directly to the victims?
regular.exp: Watering hole attacks compromise sites the victims already trust and visit voluntarily.

regular.q: An attacker registers the domain 'amaz0n-support.com' hoping confused users will land on a malicious lookalike site. What is this technique called?
regular.exp: Typosquatting registers domains that closely resemble legitimate ones to capture mistyped or confused traffic.

regular.q: A company discovers a domain nearly identical to its own, differing by a single swapped letter, hosting a fake login page. What technique does this illustrate?
regular.exp: Registering a domain that closely resembles a legitimate one to deceive users is typosquatting.

regular.q: An unauthorized person slips through a secured door right behind an employee, without that employee ever noticing. What is this called?
regular.exp: Tailgating occurs when someone follows an authorized person through a secured entrance without their knowledge; piggybacking implies the authorized person knowingly allows it.

regular.q: An employee holds a badge-secured door open for someone claiming to have left their badge at their desk, knowingly letting them into a restricted area. What social engineering technique does this represent?
regular.exp: Piggybacking is when an authorized person knowingly allows an unauthorized person to follow them through access controls.

regular.q: An attacker positions himself behind a traveler at an airport gate to watch them type their laptop password. What technique is this?
regular.exp: Shoulder surfing is directly observing someone entering sensitive information, like a password or PIN.

regular.q: An attacker digs through a company's outdoor recycling bins hoping to find printed org charts, memos, or discarded credentials. What technique is this?
regular.exp: Dumpster diving involves searching through physical trash for sensitive discarded information.

regular.q: A hospital's patient records are suddenly locked by malware, and a note demands cryptocurrency payment to restore access. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: Ransomware encrypts victim data and demands payment for the decryption key.

regular.q: Which type of malware is specifically designed to lock a victim out of their own data or systems until a ransom is paid?
regular.exp: Ransomware's defining trait is holding data or system access hostage for payment.

regular.q: A program disguises itself as a free PDF converter, and once a user installs it, it quietly opens a backdoor for the attacker. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: A trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it, unlike a worm, which spreads on its own.

regular.q: A piece of malware spreads on its own across a network by exploiting an unpatched vulnerability, needing no user interaction or host program. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: A worm self-replicates and spreads across networks independently, unlike a trojan, which requires the user to run it, or a virus, which needs a host file.

regular.q: An employee's laptop is infected with malware that silently records every keystroke and periodically uploads the log to a remote server. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: A keylogger records keystrokes, often to capture credentials, and exfiltrates them to an attacker.

regular.q: A forensic report describes malware that quietly tracks a victim's browsing history, app usage, and typed input over weeks, sending it all back to the attacker without the user ever noticing. What broad malware category does this fall under?
regular.exp: Spyware covertly gathers information about a user's activity; keyloggers are one specific type of spyware.

regular.q: An attacker plants malware that operates at the operating system kernel level, hiding its own processes and files from standard detection tools. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: Rootkits embed themselves deep in the OS, often at the kernel level, specifically to hide their presence from normal detection methods.

regular.q: Which type of malware is specifically characterized by gaining and maintaining privileged (root/admin) access while actively concealing itself from the operating system and security tools?
regular.exp: A rootkit's defining feature is privileged, stealthy persistence that evades detection.

regular.q: A disgruntled network engineer plants code configured to wipe the configuration backups automatically if her account is ever deactivated in the HR system. What is this called?
regular.exp: A logic bomb is malicious code that lies dormant until a specific triggering condition, such as a date or an event, is met.

regular.q: Which type of malicious code stays inactive until a specific condition, such as a date, event, or user action, triggers its payload?
regular.exp: Logic bombs are defined by their conditional trigger, unlike malware that activates immediately upon execution.

regular.q: An attacker systematically tries every possible password combination against a login form until one works. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: A brute force attack exhaustively tries all possible combinations until the correct credential is found.

regular.q: An admin wants to slow down attackers who are hammering a login page with thousands of password guesses per minute. Which control would be most effective here?
regular.exp: Account lockout policies, or rate limiting and backoff, restrict how many guesses an attacker can make in a given time, significantly slowing brute force attacks.

regular.q: An attacker sends small NTP queries with a spoofed source IP, the victim's address, to open servers, which then send far larger responses to the victim, saturating their bandwidth. What is this technique called?
regular.exp: Amplification attacks exploit protocols where a small request generates a much larger response, directing that response at a spoofed victim IP to multiply attack traffic.

regular.q: An analyst is trying to distinguish an amplification-based DDoS attack from a plain volumetric flood. What trait uniquely defines the amplification variant?
choices: It uses a small request to trigger a disproportionately large response directed at the victim
It only targets a single specific port
It requires physical access to the victim network
It exclusively targets DNS servers and nothing else
regular.exp: Amplification attacks are defined by the response-to-request size ratio, multiplying the attacker's effective bandwidth against the victim.

regular.q: An attacker sniffs a valid session token off the network and reuses it later to impersonate the legitimate user, all without ever learning their password. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: A replay attack captures and reuses valid credentials or session tokens to gain unauthorized access.

regular.q: Which mitigation best defends against an attacker capturing and later reusing a valid session token?
choices: Using short-lived tokens with nonces/timestamps that expire
regular.exp: Time-limited tokens and nonces make captured credentials useless shortly after capture, defeating replay attacks.

regular.q: An attacker feeds a program's input field far more data than it was designed to hold, overwriting adjacent memory and potentially achieving code execution. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: A buffer overflow occurs when input exceeds allocated memory space, corrupting adjacent memory — a classic technique behind code execution exploits.

regular.q: A code reviewer flags an input field that never checks how much data a caller submits before copying it into a fixed-size buffer. Fixing which practice would most directly close this buffer overflow risk?
choices: Using allow lists for URLs only
regular.exp: Validating and enforcing input length and bounds prevents data from exceeding allocated buffer space.

regular.q: A standard user exploits a misconfigured scheduled task running as SYSTEM to gain administrator-level access. What is this called?
regular.exp: Privilege escalation is gaining a higher level of access or permissions than originally granted, often by exploiting misconfigurations or vulnerabilities.

regular.q: A security architect wants to design a system so that even if one user account is compromised and escalated to a higher privilege, the resulting damage stays contained. Which principle achieves this?
regular.exp: Least privilege limits what any single account can access, containing the blast radius even if that account is escalated or compromised.

regular.q: An attacker manipulates a file-download parameter with sequences like '../../../../windows/win.ini' to reach files outside a web application's intended directory. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: Directory (path) traversal exploits insufficient input sanitization to access files outside the intended web root.

regular.q: A developer patching a file-download endpoint wants to stop attackers from using '../' sequences to escape the intended folder. Which fix addresses this most directly?
choices: Sanitizing and validating file path input, rejecting path-altering sequences
regular.exp: Proper input validation and sanitization of file paths prevents attackers from injecting traversal sequences like '../'.

regular.q: An attacker fires an enormous volume of legitimate-looking API calls in a short window, consuming all available server capacity and denying service to real users. What is this called?
regular.exp: Resource exhaustion attacks overwhelm a system's finite resources, such as CPU, memory, or connections, to cause a denial of service.

regular.q: Which API security control is most effective at stopping a single client from exhausting server resources with excessive requests?
regular.exp: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a given period, directly mitigating resource exhaustion.

regular.q: An attacker intercepts a connection negotiation and forces the client and server onto an older, weaker cipher suite that's far easier to break. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: A downgrade attack forces a connection to use a weaker, more vulnerable protocol or cipher version than it would otherwise negotiate.

regular.q: A pentest report recommends a fix to stop an attacker from forcing a web server's TLS negotiation down to a weak, breakable cipher. What remediation should the server team apply?
choices: Disabling support for outdated/weak protocol versions and ciphers
regular.exp: Explicitly disabling deprecated, weak protocol versions prevents an attacker from forcing a downgrade to something exploitable.

regular.q: A cryptanalyst discovers two entirely different files that produce the exact same hash digest, undermining the hash function's integrity guarantee. What is this called?
regular.exp: A hash collision occurs when two different inputs produce the same hash output, which can undermine integrity checks and digital signatures if exploitable.

regular.q: Which type of attack exploits the probability principle that finding any two matching values within a set is statistically easier than finding a match to one specific value?
regular.exp: The birthday attack leverages probability theory, the 'birthday paradox,' to find hash collisions faster than brute force would suggest.

regular.q: An attacker uses a precomputed lookup table mapping hash values back to plaintext to quickly crack a stolen, unsalted password hash. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: Rainbow tables are precomputed hash-to-plaintext lookup tables that speed up cracking unsalted hashed passwords.

regular.q: A database team wants a single change that renders precomputed rainbow tables useless against their stored password hashes. What should they implement?
regular.exp: Salting makes precomputed rainbow tables useless because each password now hashes to a unique value even if the passwords are identical.

regular.q: Instead of guessing many passwords against one account, an attacker tries a single common password, like 'Welcome2026!', against thousands of different accounts to stay under lockout thresholds. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: Password spraying tries a small number of common passwords across many accounts, staying under per-account lockout thresholds.

regular.q: A SOC analyst wants a detection strategy that catches a password spraying campaign, which a per-account lockout policy alone would completely miss. What approach should they use?
choices: Monitoring for many accounts having a small number of failed logins with the same password pattern, org-wide
Watching a single account for many failed logins
Disabling all logging to reduce noise
regular.exp: Because password spraying spreads attempts thin across many accounts, org-wide correlation, not single-account monitoring, is needed to catch it.

regular.q: A user's account signs in from Chicago and, eight minutes later, signs in again from a country halfway around the world. What indicator of compromise does this represent?
regular.exp: Impossible travel flags logins from geographically distant locations in a timeframe that would be physically impossible to travel between.

regular.q: Which type of security alert fires when authentication logs show a user account accessing resources from two locations too far apart to reach in the elapsed time?
regular.exp: This is the definition of an impossible travel indicator of compromise, often used by SIEM/UEBA tools to flag likely account compromise.

regular.q: An administrator disables unused services, closes unnecessary ports, resets default credentials, and removes unneeded software from a newly deployed server. What is this process called?
regular.exp: Hardening reduces a system's attack surface by disabling unnecessary features, services, and accounts, and enforcing secure configurations.

regular.q: A sysadmin wants to shrink a newly built server's attack surface by removing entire categories of potential entry points rather than just monitoring them more closely. Which action accomplishes this?
