regular.exp: Turning off unused ports and services removes potential attack vectors entirely, rather than just detecting or slowing an attack after the fact.

regular.q: A university and its affiliated research institutes share a single cloud environment built specifically for higher-education organizations with common compliance needs, closed to the general public. What cloud deployment model is this?
regular.exp: A community cloud is shared by several organizations with common concerns, such as compliance requirements, distinct from a single-tenant private cloud or the general-access public cloud.

regular.q: A retailer keeps its customer payment data in an on-premises data center but bursts overflow storefront traffic to a public cloud provider during the holiday rush. What cloud deployment model is this?
regular.exp: A hybrid cloud combines private or on-premises infrastructure with public cloud resources, integrated to work together.

regular.q: A platform team defines all of their servers, networks, and security groups in version-controlled configuration files that automatically stand up identical environments every time. What practice is this?
regular.exp: IaC manages and provisions infrastructure through machine-readable definition files rather than manual configuration, improving consistency and repeatability.

regular.q: A platform engineer is pitching Infrastructure as Code to leadership as a way to deploy cloud environments. Which benefit is most directly tied to adopting IaC?
choices: Elimination of the need for any access controls
Guaranteed compliance with all regulations automatically
Removal of the need for vulnerability scanning
regular.exp: IaC's core benefit is consistent, auditable, repeatable infrastructure deployment defined in code rather than manual, error-prone processes.

regular.q: An application is broken into many small, independently deployable services that each handle one specific function and talk to each other over APIs, rather than being built as one large monolithic program. What architecture is this?
regular.exp: Microservices architecture decomposes an application into small, independently deployable services, improving scalability and fault isolation but increasing API attack surface.

regular.q: An architect is weighing the security downsides of splitting a monolithic app into dozens of microservices. What tradeoff should she flag to the team?
choices: A larger overall attack surface due to many inter-service APIs
No need for authentication between services
regular.exp: While microservices improve scalability, the many API endpoints and service-to-service communications increase the number of potential attack points.

regular.q: A network engineer centrally programs and manages traffic behavior through software controllers, decoupling the control logic from the physical switching hardware. What is this called?
regular.exp: SDN separates the network control plane from the underlying data plane hardware, allowing centralized, programmatic network management.

regular.q: Which technology lets an organization dynamically reconfigure network paths and policies through centralized software rather than manually configuring each physical switch and router?
regular.exp: SDN's centralized control plane enables dynamic, programmatic network reconfiguration.

regular.q: A company places its public-facing email gateway in a separate network segment sandwiched between two firewalls, isolated from the internal corporate network, so that if it's compromised, attackers still can't reach internal systems directly. What is this segment called?
regular.exp: A screened subnet (DMZ) isolates public-facing servers between two firewall boundaries, limiting exposure of the internal network if the public server is compromised.

regular.q: A network designer needs an architecture purpose-built to host internet-facing servers while keeping them isolated from the trusted internal network. Which design fits?
regular.exp: The screened subnet (DMZ) pattern exists specifically to separate public-facing services from the internal network.

regular.q: Administrators must first authenticate to a hardened, closely monitored intermediary server before they're permitted to reach any production hosts in a sensitive network segment. What is this intermediary called?
regular.exp: A jump server (jump host) is a hardened, monitored system administrators must pass through to reach more sensitive network segments, centralizing and auditing privileged access.

regular.q: An architect wants a single, tightly controlled and logged point of entry for administrators managing servers inside a highly restricted network zone. Which device provides this?
regular.exp: Jump servers centralize and log administrative access to sensitive zones, reducing direct exposure of those systems.

regular.q: A network team wants a device deployed inline that can actively drop malicious packets in real time rather than merely alerting after the fact. What should they deploy?
regular.exp: An IPS sits inline and can actively block traffic; an IDS is typically deployed out-of-band, via a tap or mirror, and can only alert, not block.

regular.q: Why is an IDS typically deployed passively, via a tap or port mirror, rather than inline with traffic flow?
choices: Because it only monitors and alerts, and a device failure shouldn't disrupt network traffic
Because it requires physical access to every workstation
Because it cannot process encrypted traffic at all
Because it must be placed outside the firewall only
regular.exp: Since an IDS only detects and alerts rather than blocking, it's placed passively so that its failure doesn't interrupt the network traffic flow.

regular.q: An organization wants to combine WAN connectivity with security services like SWG, CASB, and ZTNA delivered from the cloud, rather than backhauling all remote traffic to a central data center. What architecture best fits this need?
regular.exp: SASE converges networking and security functions into a single cloud-delivered service, ideal for distributed remote workforces.

regular.q: Which technology lets branch offices dynamically route traffic across multiple WAN connections, such as broadband and MPLS, based on real-time performance, without manually reconfiguring routers?
regular.exp: SD-WAN uses software-defined control to intelligently route traffic across multiple WAN links based on policy and performance.

regular.q: Before a contractor's laptop is allowed onto the corporate network, a system checks it has current antivirus definitions and the latest OS patches, denying access if it doesn't comply. What is this technology called?
regular.exp: NAC enforces security policy compliance, such as patch level and antivirus status, before granting a device network access.

regular.q: Which control is specifically responsible for evaluating a device's security posture, like patch level and antivirus status, before granting it network access?
regular.exp: NAC solutions perform posture assessment and policy enforcement as a precondition for network access.

regular.q: A network architect segments the network into trust levels — untrusted internet, a semi-trusted DMZ, and a fully trusted internal zone — with defined rules governing traffic between each. What is this design approach called?
regular.exp: Security zoning divides a network into segments with differing trust levels, controlling what traffic is allowed to move between them.

regular.q: After a hardening project, a company has far fewer open ports, exposed services, and potential entry points than before. What metric has this project reduced?
regular.exp: Attack surface refers to the total sum of points where an unauthorized user could try to enter or extract data; hardening reduces it.

regular.q: A business continuity plan states that after a disaster, the reservation system must be restored within 6 hours. Which metric does this 6-hour figure represent?
regular.exp: RTO defines the maximum acceptable time to restore a system or process after a disruption.

regular.q: A backup policy states the organization can tolerate losing at most 30 minutes of transaction data during a failure, meaning backups must run at least every 30 minutes. Which metric does this reflect?
regular.exp: RPO defines the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time, which drives how frequently backups must occur.

regular.q: A power substation's control systems were engineered decades ago, run proprietary protocols, and cannot be patched without risking operational safety. What category of system is this?
regular.exp: Industrial Control Systems/SCADA manage physical processes, such as power, water, or manufacturing, and often prioritize uptime and safety over patchability, requiring compensating controls like network isolation.

regular.q: A plant's SCADA controllers can't run modern endpoint agents or accept regular patches without risking a production stoppage. What compensating control is most commonly used to protect devices like these?
choices: Requiring biometric MFA on the device itself
Running full disk encryption on the device
regular.exp: Since these devices often can't be hardened directly, isolating them on a segmented network limits their exposure and blast radius.

regular.q: A hotel configures its badge-access door controllers to unlock automatically during a power failure so guests and staff are not trapped inside during an emergency. What design principle is this?
regular.exp: Fail-open means the system defaults to an accessible/open state on failure — appropriate when safety (life/egress) outweighs security concerns.

regular.q: A jewelry store's safe lock is configured to stay locked if it loses power or communication with the central monitoring system. What design principle is this, and why might it be chosen over the alternative?
regular.exp: Fail-closed defaults to a locked/denied state on failure, prioritizing security — appropriate where unauthorized access is a bigger risk than being locked out.

regular.q: To avoid being entirely at the mercy of one cloud vendor's outages or price hikes, a company deliberately spreads critical workloads across two different cloud providers. What resilience strategy is this?
regular.exp: Platform diversity, including multi-cloud strategies, reduces single-vendor dependency and provides resilience against provider-specific outages or issues.

regular.q: What is a primary security and resilience benefit of platform diversity, such as mixing hardware vendors or cloud providers, across an environment?
choices: A single vulnerability or vendor outage is less likely to affect the entire environment
It eliminates the need for patch management entirely
It guarantees lower costs in all cases
It removes the need for a business continuity plan
regular.exp: Diversity limits the blast radius of a vendor-specific vulnerability, bug, or outage, since not all systems share the same weakness simultaneously.

regular.q: A company replicates its order database to data centers on two different continents so a regional earthquake or hurricane can't take down the entire service. What resilience concept is this?
regular.exp: Geographic dispersion spreads infrastructure across distant physical locations so a localized disaster doesn't cause total service loss.

regular.q: A multinational firm planning to spread its data centers across several countries for resilience runs into a legal snag. What consideration is most likely complicating their geographic dispersion plan?
choices: Data sovereignty laws that restrict where certain data may be stored
regular.exp: Data sovereignty laws can restrict which countries data may legally reside in, which must be balanced against geographic dispersion goals.

regular.q: A security team is weighing two controls: one deploys quickly but is difficult to patch afterward, and one takes longer to roll out but is easy to maintain. Weighing 'ease of deployment' against 'patch availability' is an example of what kind of decision?
choices: An engineering tradeoff in selecting security controls
regular.exp: Security architects constantly balance competing factors like ease of deployment, recoverability, patchability, and resource cost when selecting controls — these are engineering tradeoffs.

regular.q: When evaluating a new security control, a team weighs its power and compute overhead, how easily it can be recovered if it fails, and how easily it can be patched going forward. What category of analysis is this?
regular.exp: These are classic engineering tradeoffs weighed when selecting and deploying security controls in an architecture.

regular.q: A city government catalogs which municipal services (payroll, water billing, emergency dispatch) must keep running during a crisis and what minimum staffing and equipment each needs. What planning discipline is this?
regular.exp: COOP identifies essential functions and the resources required to keep them running during and after a disruptive event.

regular.q: Which planning activity focuses specifically on ensuring an organization's essential functions can keep operating during and after a significant disruption, distinct from simply restoring IT systems?
regular.exp: COOP is broader than disaster recovery, which focuses on IT; it addresses keeping the whole organization's essential functions running.

regular.q: A security team creates a standardized, hardened configuration template for every new Linux server, then regularly checks deployed servers against it to catch drift. What is this standardized template called?
regular.exp: A secure baseline is a documented, hardened standard configuration that new systems are built to and periodically checked against.

regular.q: A company defined a hardened secure baseline for its laptops six months ago. What ongoing work is needed to keep fleet configurations from silently drifting away from that baseline?
choices: Baseline maintenance and periodic compliance checks
One-time deployment only, with no follow-up
Disabling the baseline after initial rollout
regular.exp: Baselines must be actively maintained and re-verified over time, since configuration drift naturally occurs as systems are patched, updated, and used.

regular.q: A company requires all employee tablets accessing corporate files to have a passcode, remote wipe capability, and full-device encryption enabled before they're allowed to connect. What is this enforcement mechanism typically called?
regular.exp: MDM solutions enforce hardening requirements, such as encryption, passcodes, and remote wipe, on mobile devices before granting corporate resource access.

regular.q: An MDM policy blocks employees from installing apps from anywhere except the official app store. Which specific mobile risk does this setting directly reduce?
choices: Sideloading of malicious or unvetted applications
regular.exp: Restricting installs to official app stores, blocking sideloading, reduces the risk of installing malicious, unvetted applications.

regular.q: A security team detonates a suspicious downloaded installer inside an isolated virtual environment to observe its behavior before it ever touches production systems. What technique is this?
regular.exp: Sandboxing executes untrusted code in an isolated environment to safely observe its behavior without risking the production environment.

regular.q: A malware analyst needs to safely detonate a suspicious executable and observe exactly what it does, without any chance of infecting the production network. What technique enables this?
regular.exp: Sandboxes provide isolated execution environments specifically for safely analyzing potentially malicious code.

regular.q: An organization tracks every laptop from the moment it's purchased, through active use and ownership assignment, to its eventual secure decommissioning and disposal. What process encompasses this entire tracking effort?
regular.exp: Asset management covers the full lifecycle of a device or resource: acquisition, assignment, monitoring, and eventual decommissioning or disposal.

regular.q: A company's IT team securely wipes storage and physically destroys drives on hardware that has reached the end of its service life. Which phase of the asset management lifecycle is this?
regular.exp: Decommissioning ensures data is sanitized and hardware is disposed of securely at the end of an asset's useful life.

regular.q: A development team scans their application's source code for vulnerabilities before it's even compiled or run. What type of testing is this?
regular.exp: SAST analyzes source code or binaries without executing the program, catching issues early in development.

regular.q: A security team probes a running web application by actually sending it malicious inputs and observing the live responses, without ever seeing the source code. What type of testing is this?
regular.exp: DAST tests a running application from the outside, simulating real attacks against the live system rather than analyzing source code.

regular.q: A vulnerability scan report lists a finding with a numeric score of 9.1 out of 10, indicating extreme severity based on factors like exploitability and impact. What scoring system produced this number?
regular.exp: CVSS provides a standardized numeric score, from 0 to 10, reflecting a vulnerability's severity, used to help prioritize remediation.

regular.q: Which identifier is used as a standardized, publicly referenced name for a specific, publicly known vulnerability, such as CVE-2024-98765?
choices: A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID
regular.exp: CVE IDs uniquely and consistently identify specific publicly disclosed vulnerabilities across different tools and vendors.

regular.q: A security team pulls logs from firewalls, servers, and endpoints into one platform that correlates events and raises alerts on suspicious patterns. What type of tool is this?
regular.exp: A SIEM centralizes log collection and correlation from many sources, enabling detection of patterns that wouldn't be visible from any single log source alone.

regular.q: Which capability of a SIEM platform allows analysts to spot an attack pattern that spans multiple systems, one that no individual system log would reveal on its own?
regular.exp: Correlating events across many aggregated log sources is the core value of a SIEM, revealing multi-system attack patterns.

regular.q: A company deploys a tool that automatically blocks emails containing Social Security numbers from being sent outside the organization. What type of tool is this?
regular.exp: DLP tools detect and block sensitive data, such as PII or payment card data, from leaving the organization through unauthorized channels.

regular.q: Which control is specifically designed to detect and prevent sensitive data such as medical records or credit card numbers from being copied to a USB drive or emailed externally?
choices: A CASB used purely for SSO
regular.exp: DLP monitors and enforces policy on sensitive data movement across endpoints, email, and network egress points.

regular.q: A security agent installed on every endpoint continuously watches process behavior, flags suspicious activity beyond simple signature matching, and can automatically isolate a compromised host. What type of tool is this?
regular.exp: EDR goes beyond traditional antivirus by continuously monitoring endpoint behavior and enabling automated response actions like isolation.

regular.q: A SOC wants to correlate signals from endpoints, email, network sensors, and cloud logs into one unified detection and response platform rather than treating endpoints alone. What technology delivers this?
regular.exp: XDR broadens EDR's scope, unifying detection and response across multiple security layers rather than endpoints alone.

regular.q: When a phishing email is reported, a platform automatically pulls out indicators, checks them against threat intel feeds, quarantines matching emails org-wide, and opens a ticket — all without an analyst touching it. What type of platform enables this?
regular.exp: SOAR platforms automate and orchestrate multi-step incident response playbooks across different security tools, reducing manual analyst workload.

regular.q: A SOC manager is justifying the cost of a SOAR platform to leadership by pointing to its impact on routine, repetitive incidents. What is the primary benefit she should highlight?
choices: Faster, more consistent response with reduced manual analyst workload
Elimination of the need for any human security analysts
Guaranteed prevention of all future breaches
Removal of the need for logging
regular.exp: SOAR speeds up and standardizes incident response for repetitive tasks, freeing analysts for higher-value investigation work — it doesn't replace them entirely.

regular.q: A security tool notifies administrators whenever a critical configuration file's hash value changes unexpectedly, which could signal tampering or malware. What type of tool is this?
regular.exp: FIM tools track cryptographic hashes of critical files and alert on unauthorized or unexpected changes.

regular.q: An analyst suspects an attacker slipped a backdoor into a critical system binary. Which control would most directly have detected that modification?
regular.exp: FIM specifically detects unauthorized changes to files by comparing current hashes against known-good baselines.

regular.q: An employee signs into their corporate identity provider once and is automatically granted access to Jira, Google Workspace, and an expense-reporting tool without logging into each one separately. What concept enables this?
regular.exp: Federation and SSO allow a trusted identity provider to authenticate a user once and share that trust with multiple connected service providers.

regular.q: An architect is designing a federated SSO setup and needs a standard protocol for exchanging authentication assertions between the identity provider and each connected service. Which protocol fits?
regular.exp: SAML, and increasingly OAuth/OIDC, is a standard XML-based protocol for exchanging authentication assertions between identity and service providers.

regular.q: A bank grants access to customer account data based on a user's assigned job function — teller, loan officer, branch manager — rather than assigning permissions to each individual person. What access control model is this?
regular.exp: RBAC assigns permissions based on a user's role within the organization, simplifying management compared to per-user assignment.

regular.q: A government intelligence system enforces access based on classification labels, such as Secret and Top Secret, assigned to both users and data, with no ability for data owners to override the system's rules. What access control model is this?
regular.exp: MAC enforces access strictly based on centrally defined classification labels, with no discretion left to individual data owners — common in military and government systems.

regular.q: An organization requires that administrator credentials for production databases be checked out from a secure vault for a limited window and are automatically rotated after each use. What is this practice called?
choices: Privileged access management (PAM) with password vaulting
regular.exp: PAM solutions vault, rotate, and tightly control privileged credentials, often issuing time-limited, single-use access rather than static shared passwords.

regular.q: A PAM rollout grants an engineer elevated rights only for the duration of a specific maintenance task, then automatically revokes them. What PAM concept is being applied here?
regular.exp: Just-in-time privileged access grants elevated permissions temporarily and automatically revokes them, minimizing standing privilege risk.

regular.q: A CISO is revising the company's password policy to reflect modern guidance rather than legacy practices like frequent forced changes and mandatory special characters. What should the new policy prioritize instead?
choices: Password length and uniqueness, combined with MFA
Mandatory 30-day password rotation for all accounts
Requiring passwords to be reused across systems for consistency
regular.exp: Modern guidance, such as NIST's, favors longer, unique passwords combined with MFA over frequent forced rotation, which often leads to weaker, predictable password patterns.

regular.q: An IT department wants employees to use a long, unique password for every one of their dozens of accounts without having to memorize each one. What tool should they roll out?
regular.exp: Password managers generate and securely store unique credentials per site, removing the temptation to reuse weak passwords.

regular.q: An organization retires traditional passwords in favor of a system where users authenticate using a registered device's biometric sensor paired with a cryptographic key, with no shared secret ever transmitted. What is this approach called?
regular.exp: Passwordless authentication, such as FIDO2/WebAuthn, uses public-key cryptography and device-bound biometrics or security keys instead of shared secrets like passwords.

regular.q: A security team is pitching a move to passwordless authentication. What is the key security advantage they should cite over traditional password-based logins?
choices: They eliminate the risk of credential theft via phishing of a shared secret
They require no user device at all
They eliminate the need for any access control
They work without any registration process
regular.exp: Since no shared secret is transmitted or stored server-side in the same way, passwordless methods resist many common credential phishing and database breach attacks.

regular.q: After containing and eradicating a breach, the response team writes up what happened, what worked well, and what needs to change before next time. Which incident response phase is this?
regular.exp: The lessons learned, or post-incident review, phase captures findings to improve future preparation and response.

regular.q: Responders isolate a set of infected hosts from the rest of the network to stop the malware from spreading further, before beginning to remove it entirely. Which IR phase does this describe?
regular.exp: Containment limits the spread and impact of an incident before eradication (removal) and recovery occur.

regular.q: After resolving a security incident, the team investigates not just what happened, but why the vulnerability existed in the first place, tracing it back to a misconfigured CI/CD pipeline. What activity is this?
regular.exp: Root cause analysis digs past the immediate symptoms of an incident to identify the underlying reason it occurred, so it can be permanently fixed.

regular.q: A post-incident review spends significant time tracing an outage back to its true underlying cause rather than just noting the symptoms. Why is this step considered essential to the lessons-learned phase?
choices: It identifies the underlying issue so it can be fixed, preventing recurrence
It is required to satisfy chain of custody requirements
It replaces the need for a business impact analysis
It eliminates the need for future vulnerability scanning
regular.exp: Without addressing the true root cause, the same incident is likely to recur even after symptoms are resolved.

regular.q: Rather than waiting for an alert, a security analyst proactively digs through logs and network traffic for subtle signs of an attacker who may have already slipped past existing detection tools. What activity is this?
regular.exp: Threat hunting is a proactive search for hidden threats that automated detection tools may have missed, rather than a reactive response to alerts.

regular.q: An analyst forms a hypothesis that attackers may have pivoted through an unpatched jump server, then digs through logs specifically to confirm or rule that out. What activity is this?
regular.exp: Hypothesis-driven proactive searching for undetected threats is the defining characteristic of threat hunting.

regular.q: During incident response, a forensic analyst images RAM before imaging the hard disk, because RAM contents will vanish the moment the system is powered off. What principle guides this sequencing?
regular.exp: Order of volatility dictates collecting the most fragile, easily-lost evidence, such as RAM, cache, or network state, before more persistent evidence like disk contents.

regular.q: A forensic responder arrives at a live, still-running compromised server and must decide what evidence to capture first before it's lost. Which of these should be collected FIRST per the order of volatility?
regular.exp: CPU cache and registers, along with RAM, are the most volatile and must be captured first, before anything less fragile like disk or archived data.

regular.q: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, a company issues a notice requiring all relevant emails and documents to be preserved and shielded from routine deletion, even if the normal retention policy would otherwise purge them. What is this notice called?
regular.exp: A legal hold suspends normal data destruction and retention schedules for information relevant to anticipated or ongoing litigation.

regular.q: A records manager is confused why the standard 90-day email deletion policy must be paused for a specific custodian's mailbox once litigation is anticipated. Why does the legal hold override the normal schedule?
choices: Because destroying data relevant to anticipated litigation could constitute spoliation of evidence
Because it is required for all data at all times
Because retention policies are no longer needed once created
Because it only applies to encrypted data
regular.exp: Deleting data under legal hold can be considered spoliation of evidence, with serious legal consequences — so preservation overrides the normal retention schedule.

regular.q: A company blocks employee access to gambling and adult-content sites by category, regardless of which specific URL is requested, using a cloud-based service that inspects every outbound web request. What is this control called?
regular.exp: Web filters block or allow traffic based on URL reputation, content category, or other criteria to prevent access to malicious or inappropriate sites.

regular.q: Which control prevents users from reaching known malicious domains by intercepting and blocking the DNS resolution request for those domains before a connection is even attempted?
regular.exp: DNS filtering blocks resolution of known-malicious domains at the DNS layer, stopping connections before they can even be established.

regular.q: A document tells employees exactly what is and isn't permitted when using company laptops and network access, including a ban on installing unapproved software. What type of policy is this?
regular.exp: An AUP defines acceptable and prohibited use of organizational IT resources by employees.

regular.q: A company is drafting a document specifically to describe how it will keep essential operations running during and after a major disruption, separate from any narrower IT recovery plan. What document is this?
regular.exp: A business continuity plan focuses on sustaining critical business operations through a disruption, distinct from a narrower disaster recovery (IT-focused) plan.

regular.q: A document mandates that all passwords be at least 16 characters and rotated immediately if compromised, spelling out specific, measurable requirements that implement a broader security policy. What type of document is this?
regular.exp: Standards provide specific, mandatory technical requirements, like an exact password length, that implement the intent of a higher-level policy.

regular.q: A document offers recommended, non-mandatory best practices for securing a personal laptop, with no mechanism to enforce them. What type of document is this?
regular.exp: Guidelines are recommended, not mandatory, best practices, unlike standards or policies, which carry enforcement expectations.

regular.q: A payment processor must comply with PCI DSS requirements regardless of its own internal risk appetite, because the requirement comes from outside the organization. What category of consideration is this?
regular.exp: Regulatory requirements originate outside the organization, from government or industry bodies, and must be complied with regardless of internal preferences.

regular.q: Which factor would most directly force a multinational company to apply different data handling rules in Brazil than in the US?
choices: Regional/national legal and regulatory requirements (e.g., LGPD)
regular.exp: Region-specific laws like Brazil's LGPD are external legal considerations that override purely internal preferences on data handling.

regular.q: A manufacturing firm commissions a formal review to catalog what threats it faces, which vulnerabilities are exploitable, and what damage each scenario could cause to its assets. What process is this?
regular.exp: Risk assessment identifies and evaluates threats, vulnerabilities, and potential impacts to inform risk treatment decisions.

regular.q: Which type of risk assessment runs constantly using automated tooling rather than being performed at a single point in time?
regular.exp: Continuous assessments run constantly, often via automated tooling, as opposed to one-time, ad hoc, or periodic recurring assessments.

regular.q: A single ransomware incident is estimated to cost a company $40,000, and such incidents are expected to occur three times per year. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?
regular.exp: ALE = SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) x ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) = $40,000 x 3 = $120,000.

regular.q: An asset worth $300,000 has an exposure factor of 20% for a given threat, meaning a successful attack would destroy a fifth of its value. What is the Single Loss Expectancy (SLE)?
regular.exp: SLE = Asset Value x Exposure Factor = $300,000 x 0.20 = $60,000.

regular.q: A risk committee rates each identified risk as 'Low,' 'Medium,' or 'High' based on group discussion and judgment, rather than calculating exact dollar figures. What type of risk analysis is this?
regular.exp: Qualitative analysis uses subjective, descriptive ratings, like Low/Medium/High, rather than precise numeric or dollar calculations.

regular.q: A CFO wants a dollar figure, like an Annualized Loss Expectancy, to justify the cost of a proposed control. Which type of risk analysis produces that kind of concrete numeric output?
regular.exp: Quantitative analysis assigns actual numeric or monetary values to risk, enabling direct cost-benefit comparisons for control investments.

regular.q: A company's board states they are generally unwilling to take on any new risk unless it's necessary for survival, favoring the safest option in nearly every decision. What does this describe?
regular.exp: A conservative risk appetite reflects an organization's general unwillingness to accept risk, favoring caution over opportunity.

regular.q: A board member asks how the company's stated 'risk appetite' actually differs from its 'risk tolerance' for a specific project. What is the correct distinction?
choices: Risk appetite is the general amount of risk an org is willing to pursue; risk tolerance is the acceptable variance around a specific risk
They are two names for the exact same concept with no distinction
Risk tolerance applies only to financial risks
Risk appetite is set by external regulators only
regular.exp: Risk appetite is the broad, strategic willingness to take on risk; risk tolerance is the more specific acceptable deviation for a particular risk or metric.

regular.q: A company buys cyber insurance to cover potential losses from a data breach instead of investing heavily in additional preventive controls. What risk management strategy is this?
regular.exp: Risk transference shifts the financial impact of a risk to a third party, such as an insurance company.

regular.q: After evaluating a risky new integration with an unvetted third-party API, a company decides to scrap the integration entirely rather than accept, mitigate, or transfer the associated risk. What strategy is this?
regular.exp: Risk avoidance eliminates the risk entirely by not engaging in the risky activity at all.

regular.q: A retailer ranks its business processes by how critical they are to survival and how fast each must be restored after an outage, based on financial and operational impact. What process is this?
regular.exp: A BIA identifies critical business functions and quantifies the impact of their disruption, driving RTO/RPO targets and continuity priorities.

regular.q: A DR planning team needs to know exactly how fast the order-processing system must be brought back online after a failure. Which BIA output directly answers that question?
choices: Recovery time objective (RTO) for that system
regular.exp: BIA findings, including criticality rankings, directly drive RTO/RPO targets for each system or process.

regular.q: Before signing a contract with a new payroll vendor, a company reviews the vendor's SOC 2 report and sends a detailed security questionnaire to evaluate their controls. What is this process called?
regular.exp: Vendor assessment (due diligence) evaluates a prospective third party's security posture before entering into a business relationship.

regular.q: A customer wants contractual assurance that it can directly inspect a vendor's security controls rather than just trusting the vendor's own attestation letter. What clause grants this?
regular.exp: A right-to-audit clause explicitly grants the customer the ability to audit or inspect the vendor's environment or controls.

regular.q: Two organizations sign a document that is more formal and binding than an MOU, outlining each party's specific obligations for a joint research project, though still less detailed than a full contract. What is this document?
regular.exp: An MOA is a more formal, binding document than an MOU, specifying obligations between parties, though it typically remains less detailed than a full contract or SOW.

regular.q: Before sharing an unreleased product roadmap with a contractor, a company requires them to sign a document legally prohibiting them from disclosing that information to anyone else. What is this document?
regular.exp: An NDA legally binds a party to confidentiality regarding shared proprietary or sensitive information.

regular.q: A healthcare provider fails a HIPAA compliance audit and is fined a substantial sum, in addition to suffering significant reputational damage. What category of outcome does this illustrate?
regular.exp: Non-compliance with regulations can trigger fines, sanctions, loss of licensure, and reputational harm — all consequences organizations must weigh in governance decisions.

regular.q: A compliance officer regularly confirms and documents that the organization still meets every applicable regulatory and contractual security obligation. What ongoing activity is this?
regular.exp: Compliance monitoring is the ongoing process of verifying and documenting adherence to applicable regulations, standards, and contracts.

regular.q: A former customer emails a retailer under GDPR demanding that every piece of personal data the company holds on them be permanently erased. Which right are they invoking?
regular.exp: The right to be forgotten, or right to erasure, allows individuals to request deletion of their personal data under regulations like GDPR.

regular.q: A privacy policy repeatedly refers to 'the individual whose personal data is collected and processed by the company.' What is the correct privacy term for that individual?
regular.exp: The data subject is the individual to whom the personal data relates, distinct from the controller, who decides how data is used, and the processor, who handles it on the controller's behalf.

regular.q: A penetration tester is handed full network diagrams, source code access, and valid credentials before testing begins, to maximize testing depth and efficiency. What environment knowledge level is this?
regular.exp: A known environment (white box) test gives the tester full internal knowledge in advance, allowing deeper and more efficient testing coverage.

regular.q: Before a pentest kicks off, the client and the testing firm sign a document spelling out exactly what's in scope, when testing may occur, which techniques are off-limits, and who to call in an emergency. What is this document called?
regular.exp: Rules of engagement define the boundaries, scope, and authorized activities for a penetration test before it begins, protecting both the tester and the client.

regular.q: A security team periodically sends simulated phishing emails to staff, tracking who clicks the link and delivering just-in-time training to anyone who falls for it. What practice is this?
regular.exp: Phishing simulation campaigns test and reinforce employee awareness by sending realistic but harmless phishing attempts and training those who fail.

regular.q: A training program specifically teaches employees to forward suspicious emails to the security inbox rather than quietly deleting them. What component of a security awareness program is this?
choices: Reporting and monitoring procedures within awareness training
regular.exp: Effective awareness programs explicitly train employees on how and why to report suspected phishing or other suspicious activity, feeding the security team's detection capability.

regular.q: A Windows administrator wants to set granular per-user and per-group permissions directly on files and folders, along with built-in encryption and compression support. Which file system provides this?
regular.exp: NTFS is the modern Windows file system supporting file/folder-level permissions (ACLs), encryption, compression, and journaling, unlike older FAT-based systems.

regular.q: Which feature of NTFS lets an administrator specify exactly which users and groups can read, write, or modify a particular file, unlike simpler file systems such as FAT32?
regular.exp: NTFS stores discretionary access control lists (DACLs) on files and folders, enabling fine-grained per-user/group permission assignment.

regular.q: A user right-clicks a folder on a Windows NTFS volume and turns on a built-in feature that transparently encrypts its contents, tied to their Windows user account and certificate. What feature is this?
regular.exp: EFS is a Windows/NTFS feature that encrypts individual files and folders on a per-user basis, using a certificate tied to the user's account — distinct from whole-disk encryption like BitLocker.

regular.q: An organization needs several authorized users to each be able to decrypt the same EFS-protected file without sharing a single password. What EFS capability enables this?
choices: Adding additional authorized user certificates to the encrypted file
Switching the file system to FAT32
Enabling DNSSEC on the file server
regular.exp: EFS supports adding multiple authorized users' certificates to an encrypted file, allowing each to decrypt it independently with their own key — useful for shared organizational access.

regular.q: A wireless network from the early 2000s uses TKIP for key management to patch major flaws in its predecessor, but is itself now considered outdated compared to newer standards. What is this wireless security protocol?
regular.exp: WPA was introduced to replace the badly broken WEP, using TKIP for per-packet key mixing. It has since been superseded by WPA2 and WPA3, which use stronger encryption (AES/CCMP and SAE).

regular.q: A network engineer needs a wireless standard that fixed WEP's critical flaws but could still run on much of the same hardware after a firmware update, rather than requiring an entirely new radio. Which standard fits?
regular.exp: WPA was intentionally designed to be backward-compatible with WEP-era hardware while fixing WEP's critical key management flaws, serving as a bridge to later standards.

regular.q: A legacy application uses a 128-bit hashing algorithm to verify file integrity, but researchers have since demonstrated that two different files can be engineered to produce the same hash output. Which algorithm is this?
regular.exp: MD5 produces a 128-bit hash and is considered cryptographically broken due to practical collision attacks — two different inputs can be crafted to produce the same hash.

regular.q: A developer proposes using MD5 to hash new user passwords, but the security team rejects it. Why is MD5 no longer acceptable for security-sensitive uses like this?
choices: It is vulnerable to practical collision attacks, undermining its integrity guarantees
It is too slow for modern hardware
It does not produce a fixed-length output
It cannot process files larger than 1 MB
regular.exp: MD5's known collision vulnerabilities mean two different inputs can produce the same hash, defeating its purpose for integrity verification and signatures.

regular.q: A small office router lets dozens of internal devices, each with a private IP address, share a single public IP address when reaching the internet. What technology enables this?
regular.exp: NAT translates between private internal IP addresses and a public-facing IP address, allowing many internal devices to share one external address.

regular.q: Which technology, beyond conserving public IPv4 addresses, also provides a side benefit of obscuring the internal network structure from external hosts?
regular.exp: Because NAT hides internal private addressing behind a single public-facing address, it incidentally obscures internal network topology from outside observers.

regular.q: A small retail shop sets up its wireless access point so every employee's device connects with the exact same passphrase, which is used to derive the encryption keys. What authentication mode is this?
regular.exp: PSK mode, or WPA-Personal, uses a single shared passphrase known to all devices, unlike WPA-Enterprise, which authenticates each user individually against a RADIUS server.

regular.q: A growing company relies on a single shared PSK passphrase for wireless access across all 200 employees. What operational security drawback does this create as the company scales?
choices: The same key is shared by everyone, so it must be changed for all devices if one user leaves or the key is compromised
It requires a certificate authority for every device
It cannot be used with WPA3
It only works with wired networks
regular.exp: Because everyone shares the same key, revoking access for a single departing user or compromised device requires rotating the key across every device — unlike per-user 802.1X authentication.

regular.q: A password storage system uses a hashing algorithm from a family that produces 256-bit or 512-bit digests and is now considered much stronger than MD5, though the earliest version in the family is deprecated. What is this algorithm family?
regular.exp: The SHA family (SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3) offers stronger collision resistance than MD5, though SHA-1 itself is now deprecated in favor of SHA-2/SHA-3.

regular.q: A security standard mandates using a hashing algorithm with stronger collision resistance than either MD5 or SHA-1. Which of the following satisfies that requirement?
regular.exp: SHA-256 and the broader SHA-2/SHA-3 families provide much stronger collision resistance than both MD5 and the now-deprecated SHA-1.

regular.q: An organization subject to GDPR appoints an individual specifically responsible for overseeing data protection strategy, monitoring compliance, and serving as the point of contact for regulators and data subjects. What is this role called?
regular.exp: A DPO is a formally designated role, required under GDPR in many cases, responsible for data protection strategy, compliance oversight, and acting as a liaison with regulators and individuals.

regular.q: A regulator wants to know who at a company independently oversees privacy compliance and serves as the point of contact for data subjects and authorities, distinct from a general data owner or steward. Which role is that?
choices: Independently monitoring regulatory compliance and serving as the contact for data protection authorities
Physically storing and backing up data
regular.exp: The DPO's defining responsibilities are independent compliance oversight and acting as the liaison between the organization, regulators, and data subjects — distinct from operational data handling roles.

regular.q: An older mobile wireless application protocol (WAP) uses a lightweight security layer built for constrained mobile devices and low-bandwidth networks, serving a similar purpose to TLS on the standard web. What is this called?
regular.exp: WTLS was designed as a lightweight, resource-constrained adaptation of TLS for older WAP-based mobile devices, though it has largely been superseded by standard TLS on modern smartphones.

regular.q: Engineers designing early 2000s WAP phones couldn't just reuse standard desktop TLS. What limitation of those devices made a lighter protocol like WTLS necessary?
choices: Early mobile devices had limited processing power and bandwidth, requiring a lighter-weight security protocol
WTLS provided stronger encryption than TLS in every case
TLS could not encrypt any data at all
WTLS was required by all modern smartphone operating systems
regular.exp: WTLS was created to accommodate the limited computational resources and bandwidth of early mobile devices, which standard TLS of that era was too heavy for.

regular.q: A wireless network authenticates users via 802.1X by first building an encrypted TLS tunnel between the client and RADIUS server, then passing the user's credentials securely inside that tunnel. What authentication protocol is this?
regular.exp: PEAP wraps EAP authentication inside a protected TLS tunnel, securing the credential exchange even if the inner authentication method is weaker.

regular.q: Compared to sending raw EAP credentials with no tunnel, what specific security advantage does PEAP provide?
choices: It encrypts the authentication exchange inside a TLS tunnel, protecting credentials from interception
It removes the need for a RADIUS server entirely
It eliminates the need for any client-side configuration
It only works with wired Ethernet connections
regular.exp: By tunneling the authentication exchange inside TLS, PEAP protects credentials from being captured in transit, unlike unprotected EAP methods.

regular.q: A legacy, vendor-proprietary wireless authentication protocol predating PEAP relies on a weak challenge-response mechanism (MS-CHAP) and has been shown vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks. What protocol is this?
regular.exp: LEAP, a Cisco-proprietary predecessor to PEAP, relies on a weak MS-CHAP-based exchange that is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks, and is now considered obsolete and insecure.

regular.q: A wireless security audit flags LEAP as a legacy protocol that should be retired immediately. Why is LEAP no longer considered safe for enterprise wireless networks?
choices: Its weak credential exchange is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks, unlike its successor PEAP
It requires more bandwidth than any other EAP method
It cannot be used with RADIUS servers
It only supports wired networks, not wireless
regular.exp: LEAP's underlying MS-CHAP-based exchange is cryptographically weak and susceptible to offline dictionary/brute-force attacks, which is why PEAP and EAP-TLS replaced it.

regular.q: A network admin wants to centrally track CPU load, interface errors, and uptime across every router and switch, with alerts firing when thresholds are crossed. Which protocol is built for this?
regular.exp: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is designed for monitoring and managing network devices; SNMP traps notify a management station of significant events.

regular.q: An audit finds that network switches are still running SNMPv1 with the default 'public' community string, sending all monitoring data in cleartext. What should the admin do to fix this?
choices: Upgrade to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption enabled
regular.exp: SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption, unlike v1/v2c, which send community strings in plaintext — a common audit finding and fix.

regular.q: A tablet joins the corporate network and automatically picks up an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS settings without any manual configuration. What protocol made this possible?
regular.exp: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically assigns IP addressing and network configuration to devices joining a network.

regular.q: Employees on a floor suddenly start getting IP addresses handed out by a rogue laptop plugged into an open jack instead of the real corporate DHCP server, silently routing their traffic through the attacker. What is this attack, and what switch feature would have prevented it?
choices: DHCP spoofing; mitigated by DHCP snooping
regular.exp: A rogue DHCP server handing out malicious configuration is DHCP spoofing/starvation; DHCP snooping on switches restricts which ports may respond to DHCP requests.

regular.q: An organization wants standardized, machine-readable checklists and benchmarks to automatically verify that servers meet a security configuration baseline. What NIST framework enables this kind of automated compliance checking?
regular.exp: SCAP standardizes how vulnerability and configuration compliance data is expressed and automated, letting tools consistently check systems against defined benchmarks.

regular.q: A compliance lead is explaining to auditors what SCAP actually does within the organization's vulnerability and configuration management program. Which explanation is accurate?
choices: It encrypts data at rest on servers
It provides a standardized, automatable way to express and check security configuration and vulnerability data
It is a wireless authentication protocol
It is a backup rotation scheme
regular.exp: SCAP is about standardization and automation of security compliance/vulnerability checks, not encryption or wireless authentication.

regular.q: An employee logs into her workstation once, and from then on is silently granted access to the file server, print server, and internal wiki without re-entering her password for each one, thanks to a ticket-granting protocol behind the scenes. What protocol is this?
regular.exp: Kerberos uses a Key Distribution Center (KDC) to issue time-stamped tickets, letting clients authenticate to multiple services without repeatedly transmitting credentials.

regular.q: An attacker captures a Kerberos ticket off the wire but finds it useless an hour later when they try to replay it. What Kerberos design choice explains this?
choices: It prevents replay attacks by making old tickets expire
It eliminates the need for any authentication server
It encrypts data at rest on the client device
It replaces the need for a firewall
regular.exp: Time-stamped, expiring tickets prevent a captured ticket from being replayed successfully later — a core Kerberos security benefit.

regular.q: A company requires that a copy of every employee's disk encryption key be securely held by a trusted internal team, so data can still be recovered if an employee forgets their password or departs suddenly. What is this practice called?
regular.exp: Key escrow involves giving a trusted third party, internal or external, a copy of a cryptographic key for recovery purposes.

regular.q: A security board debating whether to adopt key escrow raises a concern about concentrating risk in one place. What is that risk?
choices: If the escrow holder is compromised, an attacker could gain access to every escrowed key
It is only compatible with symmetric encryption
It eliminates the need for access controls
regular.exp: Centralizing keys with an escrow agent creates an attractive single point of compromise — if that party is breached, all escrowed keys are at risk.

regular.q: A logistics company wants third-party certification proving it runs a documented, systematic information security management system. Which standard should it be audited against?
regular.exp: ISO 27001 specifies requirements for an Information Security Management System (ISMS) and is the standard organizations are actually certified against.

regular.q: An auditor is deciding which ISO standard a client can actually be formally certified against for its ISMS, versus which is merely supporting guidance. Which one is certifiable?
regular.exp: 27001 is the certifiable ISMS requirements standard; 27002 provides supporting control guidance but isn't itself a certification standard.

regular.q: A newly hired security engineer implementing ISO 27001 asks where to find concrete, practical guidance on actually configuring controls like access management and cryptography. Which companion standard should they consult?
regular.exp: ISO 27002 is a code of practice describing the actual controls and implementation guidance supporting ISO 27001's requirements.

regular.q: A consultant is explaining to a client how ISO 27002 relates to ISO 27001. Which description is accurate?
choices: It provides detailed control implementation guidance that supports ISO 27001's requirements
It replaces the need for ISO 27001 certification
It is a risk management standard unrelated to information security
It applies only to privacy management
regular.exp: 27002 complements 27001 by detailing how to implement the controls that 27001 requires an ISMS to address.

regular.q: A SaaS vendor already certified to ISO 27001 wants to extend its management system to formally cover privacy and personal data handling for GDPR customers. Which standard should it adopt?
regular.exp: ISO 27701 extends ISO 27001 to cover a Privacy Information Management System (PIMS), addressing PII handling and privacy obligations like GDPR.

regular.q: Which ISO standard specifically layers privacy information management requirements on top of an organization's existing information security management system?
regular.exp: 27701 is the privacy-focused extension built on top of the 27001 ISMS foundation.

regular.q: A manufacturing firm wants generic, cross-industry guidance for structuring its overall enterprise risk management process, not something scoped specifically to IT security. Which standard fits?
regular.exp: ISO 31000 provides general principles and guidelines for risk management applicable across any industry, not specifically security-focused.

regular.q: A student preparing for a governance exam needs to distinguish ISO 31000 from ISO 27001. What's the correct distinction?
choices: ISO 31000 covers general risk management principles, while ISO 27001 is specific to information security management
ISO 31000 is a certifiable standard while ISO 27001 is not
ISO 31000 only applies to privacy programs
They are two names for the exact same standard
regular.exp: 31000 is a broad, general-purpose risk management framework, whereas 27001 is specifically scoped to information security.

regular.q: A company rents virtualized servers and storage from a cloud provider but is responsible for installing and managing its own operating system, applications, and data on top of it. What service model is this?
regular.exp: IaaS provides just the raw infrastructure, such as compute, storage, and networking; the customer manages everything above that layer, including the OS.

regular.q: A company uses a fully managed CRM application where the provider handles the underlying servers, platform, and application code entirely — the company just logs in and uses it. What service model is this?
regular.exp: SaaS delivers a complete, ready-to-use application; the provider manages the infrastructure, platform, and the application itself.

regular.q: A wearable fitness tracker needs strong asymmetric encryption but has extremely limited processing power and battery life. Which type of cryptography provides equivalent security to RSA with much smaller key sizes and less computational overhead?
regular.exp: ECC provides strong security with much smaller keys than RSA, making it well-suited for resource-constrained devices like wearables and IoT sensors.

regular.q: An architect designing a fleet of battery-powered soil moisture sensors picks ECC over RSA for their public-key operations. What's the reasoning behind that choice?
choices: ECC achieves comparable security with smaller keys, reducing computation and power use
ECC is a symmetric algorithm and therefore faster
ECC does not require any key generation
RSA cannot be used for digital signatures
regular.exp: Smaller key sizes for equivalent security mean less CPU work and power draw, which matters a lot on constrained devices.

regular.q: A company wants to ensure that if its server's private key is ever compromised in the future, previously recorded TLS sessions still can't be decrypted. What property should its TLS configuration provide?
regular.exp: Perfect forward secrecy uses ephemeral session keys, via algorithms like Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral, so that compromising the long-term private key later doesn't expose previously captured traffic.

regular.q: A TLS configuration review confirms perfect forward secrecy is properly enabled. Which key exchange method must be in place for that to be true?
choices: An ephemeral (temporary, session-unique) key exchange, such as DHE or ECDHE
Reusing the same static RSA key pair for every session
Disabling encryption for the handshake only
Using a single pre-shared key for all sessions
regular.exp: Ephemeral key exchange generates a new session key each time, so no single compromised key can decrypt multiple sessions — past or future.

regular.q: An insider hides a confidential contract's contents by embedding them inside the pixel data of an ordinary-looking image file, which is then emailed out without raising suspicion. What technique was used?
regular.exp: Steganography hides the existence of data within another file, such as an image or audio file, rather than just making it unreadable, so it can bypass filters looking for obviously sensitive content.

regular.q: A trainee mixes up steganography and encryption in a report. How should the instructor correct the fundamental difference between the two?
choices: Steganography conceals the existence of the data itself, while encryption makes data unreadable without hiding that it exists
Steganography and encryption are identical techniques with different names
Steganography only works on text files
Encryption cannot be detected while steganography always can
regular.exp: Encryption scrambles data, but an observer can still see encrypted data exists; steganography tries to hide the fact that any hidden data is present at all.

regular.q: A browser trusts a website's certificate because it was signed by an intermediate CA, which was itself signed by a root CA already trusted by the operating system. What is this sequence of validation called?
regular.exp: The chain of trust links a certificate back through intermediate CAs to a trusted root CA, allowing the browser to validate authenticity without directly knowing every site's certificate.

regular.q: A CA never signs website certificates directly with its root key, instead using intermediate CAs for everyday issuance. Why is this layered approach standard practice?
choices: It keeps the highly sensitive root CA key offline and protected, limiting exposure if an intermediate is ever compromised
It makes certificates cheaper to issue
It removes the need for a chain of trust entirely
Root CAs are not capable of signing certificates directly
regular.exp: Keeping the root CA offline and using intermediates for day-to-day signing limits the damage if an intermediate is compromised — it can be revoked without invalidating the root.

regular.q: A mobile banking app is hardcoded to accept only one specific certificate, or public key, for its API server, rejecting connections even if a different, otherwise valid, trusted certificate is presented. What technique is this?
regular.exp: Certificate pinning hardcodes the expected certificate or public key in the client, protecting against attacks using a fraudulently issued but technically valid certificate from a different CA.

regular.q: A mobile app's certificate pinning implementation rejects a connection even though the presented certificate chains up to a publicly trusted CA. What kind of attack is pinning specifically designed to stop in this situation?
choices: An on-path attacker presenting a fraudulently obtained but chain-of-trust-valid certificate for the same domain
SQL injection against the app's backend database
Malware installed directly on the user's device
regular.exp: Pinning prevents the app from accepting any certificate other than the one it expects, even if an attacker somehow obtains a validly-signed certificate for that domain from a different CA.

regular.q: A startup wants the strong isolation of a hardware security module for its encryption keys but doesn't want to purchase, rack, and maintain physical HSM appliances. What cloud offering provides this?
choices: A cloud Key Management Service (KMS) backed by HSMs
regular.exp: Cloud KMS offerings let organizations manage keys with HSM-backed protection without owning the physical hardware, billed as a managed service.

regular.q: A security committee debating a move from on-prem HSMs to a cloud KMS raises a concern about control. What tradeoff should they weigh?
choices: You are trusting the cloud provider's operational and access controls around your keys, rather than controlling the hardware directly
Cloud KMS cannot encrypt or decrypt any data
On-premises HSMs are always cheaper at any scale
Cloud KMS eliminates the need for any access control policies
regular.exp: Using a managed KMS means trusting the provider's security and operational practices for key protection, a meaningful shift in control compared to owning physical HSM hardware.

regular.q: A genomics research firm wants a cloud provider to run computations on patient DNA data without ever being able to see the underlying unencrypted values, even during processing. What emerging cryptographic technique enables computing directly on encrypted data?
regular.exp: Homomorphic encryption allows mathematical operations to be performed directly on ciphertext, producing an encrypted result that, when decrypted, matches the result of the same operations on the plaintext, without ever exposing the plaintext to the processor.

regular.q: A pharmaceutical company outsources statistical analysis of trial data to a cloud vendor using homomorphic encryption. What's the security payoff of that approach?
choices: The third party can compute on the data without ever needing to decrypt or view the underlying plaintext
It makes processing faster than working with plaintext data
It eliminates the need for any access controls on the third party's systems
It replaces the need for TLS during data transmission
regular.exp: Because computation happens directly on ciphertext, the processing party never has access to the sensitive plaintext, significantly reducing exposure risk.

regular.q: Before rolling out a router configuration change, the network team stores the exact previous configuration in a versioned repository so it can be restored instantly if the change causes problems. What practice supports this kind of reliable backout capability?
regular.exp: Version-controlling configuration changes gives change management a reliable, exact record to roll back to, supporting the backout plan requirement of a formal change process.

regular.q: A change management audit praises the network team for satisfying the backout plan requirement thoroughly. How does version control specifically enable that?
choices: It preserves an exact historical record of prior configurations that can be restored quickly if a change fails
It automatically approves all changes without review
It prevents any changes from ever being made
It replaces the need for a change advisory board
regular.exp: Having a precise, retrievable history of past configurations is what makes a fast, reliable rollback possible when a change doesn't go as planned.

regular.q: An attacker posts a product review containing a malicious script tag. When other shoppers view the page, the script runs in their browsers, stealing their session cookies. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: XSS injects malicious script into a web page viewed by other users, executing in their browser context and often used to steal session cookies or hijack sessions.

regular.q: A developer patching a forum app wants to stop stored XSS from user-submitted posts. Which fix actually closes the hole?
choices: Properly encoding/escaping user-supplied output before rendering it in HTML
Disabling HTTPS on the login page
Allowing all JavaScript from any domain to run
regular.exp: Output encoding ensures user-supplied content is rendered as inert text or data rather than executable script, directly preventing XSS.

regular.q: A web form that runs a system traceroute command using unsanitized user input lets an attacker append '; rm -rf /' to the input field, causing the underlying OS to execute the extra command. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: Command injection occurs when unsanitized user input is passed directly to an OS shell or command interpreter, allowing arbitrary command execution.

regular.q: An application must shell out to a system utility with user-supplied filenames. Which practice most directly prevents command injection in this scenario?
choices: Avoiding direct OS shell calls with user input, or strictly validating/escaping input against an allow list
regular.exp: Avoiding shell invocation with untrusted input, or rigorously validating and escaping it, closes off the ability for an attacker to append extra commands.

regular.q: A file permission check runs, and then, before the file is actually used, an attacker swaps it out for a malicious file in the brief window between the check and the use. What class of vulnerability is this?
regular.exp: TOCTOU race conditions exploit the gap between when a condition is checked and when it's acted upon, letting an attacker change the state in between.

regular.q: A code reviewer flags a function that checks a file's permissions, then opens it moments later, as vulnerable to a TOCTOU race. Which fix would actually eliminate the vulnerability?
choices: Performing the check and the action atomically, as a single, uninterruptible operation, rather than as two separate steps
Disabling multi-threading entirely in all cases
regular.exp: Making check-then-act sequences atomic removes the window of opportunity an attacker needs to interfere between the two steps.

regular.q: An attacker compromises a host and runs malicious code entirely in memory using legitimate tools like PowerShell, never writing an executable to disk, making traditional signature-based antivirus far less effective. What type of malware is this?
regular.exp: Fileless malware operates in memory using legitimate system tools, living off the land, leaving little to no trace on disk for traditional file-scanning antivirus to detect.

regular.q: A traditional antivirus product completely misses an attack that ran entirely through PowerShell in memory. Why did the AV fail to catch it?
choices: It resides in memory and abuses legitimate system tools rather than writing a distinct malicious file to disk
It requires physical access to install
It cannot execute any code at all
regular.exp: Without a malicious file on disk to scan and fingerprint, traditional signature-based detection has little to work with — behavioral or EDR-based detection is far more effective against it.

regular.q: An attacker forces a legitimate running process to load and execute a malicious dynamic-link library, letting the malicious code run under the identity and permissions of the trusted process. What technique is this?
regular.exp: DLL injection loads malicious code into the address space of a legitimate process, letting the attacker's code run with that process's permissions and blend in with legitimate activity.

regular.q: An attacker chooses to inject a malicious DLL into an already-trusted, running process rather than dropping a new standalone executable. What advantage does this give them?
choices: It lets malicious code inherit the trusted process's permissions and blend in, evading detection tools that trust that process
It is the only way to execute any code on Windows
It requires no privileges at all to perform
It automatically encrypts all network traffic
regular.exp: Running inside a trusted process's context helps malicious activity evade security tools that whitelist or trust that legitimate process.

regular.q: A disgruntled employee with legitimate access to the payroll system quietly exports the entire salary table to a personal cloud drive before resigning. What category of threat does this represent?
regular.exp: An insider threat comes from someone with legitimate authorized access — an employee, contractor, or partner — misusing that access, whether intentionally or accidentally.

regular.q: A security team wants to catch an employee who has legitimate access silently exporting far more customer data than usual. What control is best suited to detecting this kind of activity?
choices: User and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) monitoring for anomalous data access/export patterns
regular.exp: Because the access itself is authorized, signature-based tools won't flag it — behavioral analytics that detect deviations from a user's normal pattern are what catches this kind of insider activity.

regular.q: Attackers compromise a widely used software vendor's build pipeline and slip malicious code into a legitimate update, which is then automatically installed by thousands of the vendor's customers. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: Supply chain attacks compromise a trusted upstream vendor or component, letting attackers reach many downstream victims through a single trusted distribution channel.

regular.q: A CISO explains to the board why a single compromised software vendor is a bigger worry than a direct attack on their own network. What's the core reasoning?
choices: Compromising one trusted vendor can provide access to every one of that vendor's downstream customers simultaneously
They require no technical skill to execute
They are always detected immediately by antivirus
regular.exp: A single successful supply chain compromise can cascade to a huge number of victims who all trusted the same upstream source, multiplying the attack's impact.

regular.q: A prankster at a coffee shop sends anonymous, unsolicited pop-up messages to nearby phones with Bluetooth discovery turned on, without ever accessing anything stored on them. What is this activity called?
regular.exp: Bluejacking is sending unsolicited messages or data to Bluetooth devices; it's a nuisance but doesn't involve unauthorized data access.

regular.q: An attacker exploits a flaw in an old Bluetooth headset's pairing implementation to silently pull contacts and text messages off a nearby phone. What is this attack called?
regular.exp: Bluesnarfing involves unauthorized access to data, such as contacts, messages, or files, on a Bluetooth device, unlike the merely annoying bluejacking.

regular.q: An attacker floods a cafe's wireless access point area with spoofed deauthentication frames, forcibly disconnecting legitimate clients so they'll reconnect to a malicious rogue access point instead. What type of attack is this?
regular.exp: Deauthentication attacks abuse unauthenticated 802.11 management frames to forcibly disconnect clients, often as a precursor to an evil-twin or credential-capture attack.

regular.q: Right after an attacker sends a burst of forged deauth frames at a coffee shop's access point, what does the attacker typically hope will happen next?
choices: Getting the disconnected clients to reconnect to an attacker-controlled rogue/evil-twin access point
Sending spam email from the victim's account
Performing a SQL injection against a database
regular.exp: Forcing a disconnect is often used to push victims toward reconnecting to a malicious access point that can capture credentials or traffic.

regular.q: A legacy wireless network still uses an encryption protocol with a small, statically reused initialization vector, which researchers demonstrated could be cracked within minutes using freely available tools. What protocol is this?
regular.exp: WEP's small, reused initialization vectors and weak RC4 implementation make it trivially crackable with modern tools — it should never be used today.

regular.q: A student asks why WEP was so easy to crack compared to WPA2 despite both technically using encryption. What was the actual cryptographic flaw?
choices: Its small, frequently reused initialization vectors led to predictable keystreams that could be statistically analyzed and cracked
It used no encryption at all
It required a certificate authority for every connection
It only worked over wired connections
regular.exp: WEP's short, reused IVs created patterns in the keystream that attackers could exploit to recover the key relatively quickly.

regular.q: A traveler at a crowded train station has their contactless transit card data silently read and duplicated by someone brushing past with a hidden RFID reader. What risk does this illustrate?
regular.exp: RFID/NFC signals can potentially be read and cloned by nearby unauthorized readers if not properly protected, such as with shielding or encryption — a real risk for proximity access badges and contactless payment cards.

regular.q: A security team wants to protect employee badges from being skimmed by a hidden reader in a crowded lobby. What mitigation directly addresses this?
choices: Using an RFID-blocking sleeve/wallet and encrypted badge technology
Disabling the badge reader at the front door
Increasing the badge's Wi-Fi signal strength
Using a longer PIN on the badge
regular.exp: RFID-blocking materials physically prevent unauthorized scanning at a distance, and encrypted badge protocols prevent simple cloning even if signals are intercepted.

regular.q: An attacker takes a large list of usernames and passwords leaked from a breach at a retail site and automatically tries them against a completely different company's login page, relying on users reusing the same password across sites. What attack is this?
regular.exp: Credential stuffing reuses known, previously breached username/password pairs against other sites, exploiting password reuse rather than guessing new passwords.

regular.q: A login portal keeps getting hit with valid username/password pairs pulled from an unrelated third-party breach. Which control most effectively neutralizes this credential stuffing threat?
choices: Requiring multi-factor authentication in addition to password login
regular.exp: Even if a correct username/password pair is stuffed successfully, MFA blocks the attacker without the second factor — directly neutralizing the core risk of reused credentials.

regular.q: An attacker who has compromised a Windows workstation extracts a cached password hash and uses it directly to authenticate to other systems on the network, never needing to crack the hash into plaintext. What attack is this?
regular.exp: Pass-the-hash exploits authentication protocols that accept the hash itself as proof of identity, letting an attacker authenticate without ever knowing the actual plaintext password.
