pbq.exp: Each generation fixed a specific weakness in its predecessor: WPA patched WEP's IV problem with TKIP, WPA2 replaced TKIP with real AES encryption, and WPA3 added SAE to resist offline password-guessing even against a captured handshake.

pbq.q: Drag each authentication example to the factor category it represents.
pbq.exp: The four common authentication factor categories are knowledge (know), possession (have), inherence (are), and behavior (do) — true MFA combines factors from different categories, not just different examples of the same one.

pbq.topic: PBQ: Malware Type to Defining Trait
pbq.q: Drag each malware type to the trait that best defines it.
pairs: Self-replicates and spreads across a network without user interaction
Disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it
Hides its presence by embedding at the OS/kernel level
Stays dormant until a specific trigger condition is met
pbq.exp: Each malware category is defined by a distinct behavior: worms self-propagate, trojans rely on deception to get installed, rootkits focus on stealth/persistence, and logic bombs wait for a trigger before activating.

pbq.q: Drag each social engineering technique to its correct description.
pairs: Social engineering conducted over a phone call
Social engineering conducted via text message
Fabricating a false scenario to obtain information
Following an authorized person through a secured door without their knowledge
pbq.exp: These techniques differ mainly in delivery channel and method: vishing/smishing are voice/SMS-based phishing, pretexting relies on a fabricated story, and tailgating is a physical-access technique.

pbq.q: Drag each network topology to its correct description.
pairs: All devices connect to a central switch or hub
Every device connects to every other device for maximum redundancy
All devices share a single central cable, now largely legacy
Each device connects to exactly two neighbors, forming a closed loop
pbq.exp: Topology determines how devices are physically/logically interconnected; star is the dominant modern LAN design, mesh maximizes redundancy at the cost of complexity, and bus/ring are largely legacy designs today.

pbq.q: Drag each VPN type/mode to its correct description.
pairs: Connects two entire office networks over the internet
Connects an individual remote user's device into the corporate network
Only routes corporate-bound traffic through the tunnel
Routes all client traffic through the tunnel
pbq.exp: Site-to-site and remote-access describe who's being connected (networks vs. individual users), while split- and full-tunnel describe how much of that connection's traffic actually goes through the encrypted tunnel.

pbq.q: Drag each data classification level to an example of data that would typically fall under it.
pairs: Trade secrets and data under legal hold
pbq.exp: Classification levels scale from data meant for open distribution (public) up to data requiring the tightest controls (restricted), guiding how each category must be handled and protected.

pbq.q: Drag each physical security control to the purpose it primarily serves.
pairs: Stop vehicle-borne attacks while allowing pedestrian traffic
Ensures only one authenticated person passes through at a time
Deters intruders and improves surveillance visibility at night
Provides active human judgment and response at a checkpoint
pbq.exp: Physical controls range from passive/structural (bollards, lighting) to active/procedural (mantraps enforcing one-at-a-time entry, guards providing judgment-based response).

pbq.q: Drag each step of the vulnerability management lifecycle to its correct description.
pairs: Running scans to discover vulnerabilities across the environment
Assessing severity, exploitability, and business impact
Applying patches or compensating controls to fix the issue
Re-scanning to confirm the vulnerability is actually resolved
pbq.exp: Vulnerability management is a continuous cycle: find issues, prioritize by real risk (not just raw severity score), fix them, then verify the fix actually worked before considering it closed.

pbq.q: Drag each characteristic to whether it describes IPv4 or IPv6.
pairs: Address exhaustion solved short-term via NAT/CIDR
Vastly larger address space, eliminating the need for NAT
pbq.exp: IPv4's 32-bit space (about 4.3 billion addresses) has been effectively exhausted and is stretched further via NAT/CIDR; IPv6's 128-bit space is large enough that NAT is no longer necessary for address conservation.
